---
<!-- theorem--1: body_md -->
Let $\overline{M}$ be a globally hyperbolic spacetime with timelike boundary, let $V$ be a smooth function on $\overline{M}$, and let
	\begin{equation*}
	P=\Box_g+V
	\end{equation*}
	be a scalar, formally self-adjoint, normally hyperbolic operator of order two with Dirichlet boundary condition. Then the corresponding Dirichlet field algebra admits a Dirichlet--Hadamard state.
<!-- end theorem--1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lemma:exact sequence of distributions}
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item The following sequence is exact
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:exact sequence for supported/extensible distributions}
			0\to \dot\mathscr{D}'_{\partial M}(\overline{M})\hookrightarrow\dot\mathscr{D}'(\overline{M})\xrightarrow{\cdot|_M}\{u|_{M}\colon u\in\mathscr{D}'(\overline{M})\}\to 0,
		\end{equation}
		\item A distribution $u\in\mathscr{F}(M)$ is in ${\mathscr{F}}(\overline{M})$ if, and only if, for any enlargement $N\supset \overline{M}$ we find $U\in\mathscr{F}(N)$ such that $U|_{M}=u$.
		\item A distribution $u\in\mathscr{F}(M)$ is in $\dot\mathscr{F}(\overline{M})$ if, and only if, for any enlargement $N\supset \overline{M}$ we have $\widetilde{u}\in \mathscr{F}(N)$, where $\widetilde{u}(\varphi)=u(\varphi|_{M})$ for all $\varphi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(N)$ is the ``extension-by-zero'' of $u$.
		\item In particular, on any enlargement $N$ of $\overline{M}$, the ``extension-by-zero'' of supported distributions $u\in\dot\mathscr{F}(\overline{M})$ realises them as elements of $\mathscr{F}(N)$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lemma:conormal+dual-conormal=smooth}
	We have
	\begin{equation}
		\dot\mathscr{A}(\overline{M})\cap\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})=\mathscr{A}(\overline{M})\cap\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})=\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M}).
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\cref{lemma:conormal+dual-conormal=smooth} (1) is an instance of the principle that the regularity of a distribution can be established by looking separately at tangential and normal directions (see for example \cite{de_gosson_microlocal_1982}). However, distributions in $\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$, while admitting distributional traces at $\partial M$ of all orders, are not in general ``smooth in $x$'' (see \cref{example:A' vs N'} below).
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lemma:domains of powers of Laplacian}
	We have
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item For every $s\in[0,1]$, $\mathcal D_s=\dot\mathsf{H}^s(\overline{M})$;
		\item For every $s\in[-1,0]$, $\mathcal D_s=\mathsf{H}^{s}(\overline{M})$;
		\item For every $s\in\mathbb{R}$, $\dot\mathsf{H}^s(\overline{M})=\mathsf{H}^{-s}(\overline{M})'$ with respect to the $L^2(M)$ pairing.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:symplectic domain of Laplacian}
	For every $s\in[-1,1]$, in particular for $s=1/2$, the space $\dot\mathsf{H}^s(\overline{M})\oplus\mathsf{H}^{-s}(\overline{M})$ is a symplectic vector space.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Any vector space of the form $V\oplus V'$ is symplectic with respect to $\omega((f,\alpha),(h,\beta))=\braket{\alpha, h}-\braket{\beta, f}$. Since $\dot\mathsf{H}^s(\overline{M})=\left(\mathsf{H}^{-s}(\overline{M})\right)'$, the proof is complete.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{remark:sobolev spaces}
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item The space $\dot\mathsf{H}^{1/2}(\overline{M})$ is the classical space $\mathsf{H}^{1/2}_{00}(M)$ of Lions and Magenes. See Theorem 11.7 in \cite{lions_non-homogeneous_1972_I} for an explicit definition via Gagliardo seminorms and the characterisation as interpolation space in the scale $\mathsf{H}^s_0(\overline{M})$.
		\item Since the boundary is smooth, $\dot\mathsf{H}^s(\overline{M})=\widetilde{\mathsf{H}}^s(\overline{M})$ for every $s\in\mathbb{R}$ in the notation of \cite{mclean_strongly_2000}, which reconciles \cref{lemma:domains of powers of Laplacian} with Theorem 3.30 in the reference.
		\item Notice that $\mathcal D_s\neq\dot\mathsf{H}^s(\overline{M})$ and $\mathcal D_{-s}\neq\mathsf{H}^{-s}(\overline{M})$ if $s$ is sufficiently large. Indeed we have $\bigcap_{s}\dot\mathsf{H}^s(\overline{M})=\dot{\mathit C}^{\infty}(\overline{M})$, while for elements of $\bigcap_s\mathcal D_s$ only $\gamma_0 A^j u$ has to vanish. This is related to the fact that $\operatorname{\mathrm{dom}}(\Delta_D^k)\subsetneq\dot\mathsf{H}^1(\overline{M})\cap\mathsf{H}^{2k}(\overline{M})$ for $k\ge 2$, since the smaller space encodes boundary conditions of higher order. For our discussion of $s=1/2$ this does not play a role.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lemma:symplectic domain of laplacian - noncompact}
	For any $s\in \mathbb{R}$, the space $\mathcal D_s\oplus\mathcal D_{-s}$ is symplectic.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lemma:restriction and Sobolev spaces}
	Consider the restriction map to $M$ as in \cref{lemma:exact sequence of distributions}. For any $s\in\mathbb{R}$, it extends to bounded operators
	\begin{align*}
		\dot\mathsf{H}^s_\mathrm{comp}(\overline{M})&\to \mathsf{H}^s_\mathrm{comp}(\overline{M})\\
		\dot\mathsf{H}^s_\mathrm{loc}(\overline{M})&\to \mathsf{H}^s_\mathrm{loc}(\overline{M}).
	\end{align*}
	Moreover, the above extensions are surjective if $s<1/2$ and injective if $s >-1/2$, so they are in particular isomorphisms in the range $s\in(-1/2,1/2)$.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
Let $K\subset\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+}$ be compact. We have:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\mathscr{D}'_K(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\mathbb{R}}x^\alpha\mathsf{H}^{-\infty}_{b,K}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$;
		\item $\mathscr{A}_K(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\mathbb{R}}x^\alpha \mathsf{H}^{\infty}_{b,K}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$;
		\item $\dot\mathscr{A}'_K(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})=\bigcap_{\alpha\in\mathbb{R}}x^\alpha \mathsf{H}^{-\infty}_{b,K}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$;
		\item $\dot{\mathit C}^{\infty}_K(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})=\bigcap_{\alpha\in\mathbb{R}}x^\alpha\mathsf{H}^{\infty}_{b,K}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:mellin and supported distributions}
	The Mellin transform is not injective on $\dot\mathscr{D}'(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$, since its kernel is exactly $\dot\mathscr{D}'_{\{x=0\}}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$: if $U,V\in\dot\mathscr{D}'(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$ and $u=U-V\in\dot\mathscr{D}'_{\{x=0\}}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$, then near each point $p\in \{x=0\}$ we have $u=\sum_{k=0}^Na_k(y)\partial^k\delta(x)$ for some distributions $a_k$ on $\{x=0\}$. For large $\Im \lambda$, pairing this against $x^{-\mathrm{i}\lambda-1}$ makes sense and returns 0, irrespective of $\lambda$. As we will see below, $\mathcal{M} u(\lambda)$ depends complex analytically on the parameter, therefore $\mathcal{M} u$ is the zero function. Therefore, $\mathcal{M} (U)$ only depends on the equivalence class of $U$ in $\mathscr{D}'(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$. In view of \cref{lemma:conormal+dual-conormal=smooth}, injectivity is restored for dual-conormal distributions. This is the crux of why we can test the $b$-wave-front set via $\mathcal{M}$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lemma:properties of Mellin transform}
	We have:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Whenever both sides make sense, $\mathcal{M}[(xD_x)u](\lambda)=\lambda\widehat{u}(\lambda)$ and, for all $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$, $\mathcal{M}[x^\alpha u](\lambda)=\widehat{u}(\lambda+\mathrm{i}\alpha)$;
		\item $\mathcal{M}\operatorname{\mathcal F}\colon x^\alpha\mathsf{H}^s_b\to \braket{(\Re\lambda,\eta)}^{-s}L^2(\{\Im\lambda={-\alpha}\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n-1})$ is an isometric isomorphism, in particular $\mathcal{M}\operatorname{\mathcal F}\colon L^2(\frac{dx}{x}dy)\xrightarrow{\sim}L^2(d\xi d\eta)$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{theo:paley-wiener for extensible}
		The Mellin transform of a distribution $u\in\mathscr{E}'(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$ satisfies the following:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item There exists $R>0$ such that, for all $\lambda$ for which $\mathcal{M} u$ is defined, $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}\mathcal{M} u(\lambda)\subset B(0,R)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$;
		\item There exist constants $C_1, C_2, r, N>0$ such that
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:paley-wiener bound}
			\|\mathcal{M} u(\lambda)\|_{\mathsf{H}^{-r}(\mathbb{R}^{n-1})}\leq C_1e^{C_2|\Im \lambda|}(1+|\lambda|)^{N}.
		\end{equation}
	\end{enumerate}
	Conversely, if a $\mathscr{D}'(\mathbb{R}^{n-1})$-valued function, holomorphic in a half-plane $\Im\lambda>K$, satisfies the two conditions above, then it is the Mellin transform of a unique $u\in\mathscr{E}'(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{theo:paley-wiener for conormal}
	A distribution $u\in\mathscr{E}'(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$ is in $\mathscr{A}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$ if, and only if,
	its Mellin transform $\mathcal{M} u$ takes values in smooth functions on $\mathbb{R}^{n-1}$ with rapid decay (together with all their derivatives) along every horizontal line in the half-plane on which it is holomorphic.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{theo:paley-wiener for dual-conormal}
	A distribution $u\in\mathscr{E}'(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$ is in $\mathscr{A}'(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$ if, and only if, $\mathcal{M} u$ extends to a meromorphic function with simple poles at $-\mathrm{i}\mathbb{N}$, which has the property: for every $L>0$ we find $C,r>0$ such that if $|l|\leq L$
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:paley-wiener for dual-conormal}
		\left\|\prod_{j=0}^{\lfloor L\rfloor}(\xi+\mathrm{i} (l+j))\mathcal{M} u(\xi+\mathrm{i} l)\right\|_{\mathsf{H}^{-r}}\leq  C\braket{\xi}^{r}.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{theo:mellin transform of A'}
	Assume $u\in\mathscr{A}'([0,\infty)^2\times\mathbb{R}^{n-2})$ has compact support. Then its Mellin transform $\mathcal{M}{u}$ defines a unique meromorphic function
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:dual-conormal has mermorphic Mellin}
		\mathbb{C}^2\setminus (-\mathrm{i}\mathbb{N}\times \mathbb{C}\cup\mathbb{C}\times -\mathrm{i} \mathbb{N})\to \mathscr{E}'(\mathbb{R}^{n-2}),
	\end{equation}
	such that
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item for all $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}^2\setminus(-\mathrm{i}\mathbb{N}\times \mathbb{C}\cup\mathbb{C}\times -\mathrm{i} \mathbb{N})$, $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} \mathcal{M}{u}(\lambda,\cdot)\subset B(0,R)\subset\mathbb{R}^{n-2}$ for some $R>0$ not depending on $\lambda$;
		\item for every $\epsilon>0$ there exists an integer $p$ and positive constants $C_1,N,C_2$ such that for all $\lambda, \mu$ with $\Im\lambda,\Im\mu\ge \epsilon >0$ we have
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:subexponential bound of Mellin transform}
			\|\mathcal{M}(u)(\lambda,\mu,\,\cdot\,)\|_{\mathsf{H}^{-p}}\leq C_1e^{C_2(|\Im \lambda|+|\Im\mu|)}\braket{(\Re\lambda,\Re\mu)}^{N}.
		\end{equation}
	\end{enumerate}
	In this case, on every strip $\{|\Im\lambda|,|\Im\mu|\leq L\}$ and denoting by $\eta$ the Fourier variable of $y$, the Fourier transform of $\prod_{j=0}^{\lfloor L\rfloor}(\lambda+\mathrm{i} j)(\mu+\mathrm{i} j)\mathcal{M}(u)$, as a family of distributions on $\mathbb{R}^{n-2}$, is polynomially bounded in $\braket{(\Re\lambda,\Re\mu,\eta)}$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:b-wave-front set}
	Let $u\in\mathscr{D}'(\overline{M})$. We say that $(x_0,y_0,\xi_0,\eta_0)\notin\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$ if there exists a cutoff $\chi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$, $\chi\equiv1$ near $(x_0,y_0)$, an open cone $\Gamma\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}$ around $(\xi_0,\eta_0)$, and an $L>0$ such that $\mathcal{M} (\chi u)(\lambda)$ is holomorphic in a neighbourhood of the line $\{\Im  \lambda=L\}$ and, for all $(\xi,\eta)\in \Gamma$ and all $N\in\mathbb{N}$, we find a constant $C_{N\chi\Gamma}$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:b-wave-front set}
		|\widehat{\chi u}(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)|\le C_{N\chi\Gamma} \braket{(\xi,\eta)}^{-N}.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lemma:independence of the line}
	For some $\varepsilon>0$ let $f\colon \{a-\varepsilon< \Im z< b+\varepsilon\}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a holomorphic function, polynomially bounded in $\Re z$ on the closed substrip $\{a\leq \Im z\leq b\}$. Assume furthermore that $f$ is rapidly decreasing along the line $\Im z=a$. Then $f$ is rapidly decreasing along every line $\Im z=l$ for $l\in (a,b)$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
It suffices to prove the lemma for the case $a=0$, $b=1$, $L=0$. It also suffices to show that we have rapid decay along $\Im z=1/2$. Choose $k$ so that $|f(z)|\leq C|z+\mathrm{i}|^{k}$ is bounded on the strip (the existence of $k$ is guaranteed by the assumed polynomial control). We will apply Hadamard's three lines theorem to deduce that $f$ is rapidly decaying along every line in the strip $\Im z\in(a,b)$. For an arbitrary $N\in \mathbb{N}$, let $K>\max (N,k)$. On the strip, we have $1-\mathrm{i} z\neq 0$ and $|1-\mathrm{i} z|\sim 1+|\Re z|\sim\braket{\Re z}$. Setting for any $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$
	\begin{equation}
		F_\alpha(z)\equiv f(z)(1-\mathrm{i}(z-\alpha))^{-K},
	\end{equation}
	we have that $F_\alpha$ is bounded and holomorphic on the strip. On the sides of the strip we estimate as follows. First, if $\Im z=0$, we know that $f(z)$ is rapidly decaying as $|z|\to\infty$. Second, Peetre's inequality gives that $\braket{x-\alpha}^{-K}\lesssim \braket{x}^K\braket{\alpha}^{-K}$. Thus we find
	\begin{align*}
		\sup_{\Im z=0}|F_\alpha(z)|&\lesssim \sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|f(x)(1+|x-\alpha|)^{-K}|\lesssim |f(x)|\braket{x-\alpha}^{-K}\\
		&\lesssim |f(x)|\braket{x}^K\braket{\alpha}^{-K}\lesssim \alpha^{-K}.
	\end{align*}
	On the other hand, for $\Im z=1$, notice that $\braket {x-\alpha}^{-K}=\braket{x-\alpha}^{-m}\braket{x-\alpha}^{m-K}$ with the second factor bounded. If we use Peetre's inequality to get $\braket{x-\alpha}^{-m}\lesssim \braket{x}^{-m}\braket{\alpha}^{m}$, we deduce
	\begin{align*}
		\sup_{\Im z=1}|F_\alpha(z)|&\lesssim \braket{x}^m \braket{x-\alpha}^{-K}\\
		&\lesssim \braket{x}^m\braket{x-\alpha}^{-m}\lesssim \braket{\alpha}^m.
	\end{align*}
	We now apply Hadamard's three-lines theorem to $F_\alpha$ along a line $\Im z=l\in (0,1)$ to see that
	\begin{equation*}
		|F_\alpha(\alpha+\mathrm{i} l)|\lesssim \braket{\alpha}^{-K(1-l)+ml}.
	\end{equation*}
	Since the factor $|(1-\mathrm{i}(z-\alpha))|^{-K}=|1+l|^{-K}$ is bounded in the strip, we obtain
	\begin{equation*}
		|f(\alpha+\mathrm{i} l)|\lesssim \braket{\alpha}^{-K(1-l)+ml}.
	\end{equation*}
	Since $K$ can be chosen arbitrarily large, we see that $f$ decays rapidly along the line $\Im z=l$ for any $l\in(0,1)$. This finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
Let $u\in\mathscr{D}'(\overline{M})$. We say that $(x_0,y_0,\xi_0,\eta_0)\notin\mathsf{WF}_b^s(u)$ if there exists a cutoff $\chi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$, $\chi=1$ near $(x_0,y_0)$, a conic cutoff $\psi$, $\psi=1$ near $(\xi_0,\eta_0)$, supported in an open cone $\Gamma\subset \mathbb{R}^{n}\setminus\{0\}$ around $(\xi_0,\eta_0)$, and an $L>0$ such that $\mathcal{M} (\chi u)(\lambda)$ is holomorphic in a neighbourhood of $\{\Im \lambda=L\}$ and
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Sobolev b-wave-front set}
		\psi(\Re\lambda,\eta)\braket{(\Re \lambda,\eta)}^s\widehat{\chi u}(\Re\lambda+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^{n}).
	\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lemma:ordinary and sobolev wave-front set}
	For any $u\in \mathscr{D}'(\overline{M})$ we have
	\begin{align*}
		\mathsf{WF}_b^s(u)&\subseteq \mathsf{WF}_b^{r}(u),\quad s\leq r,\\
		\mathsf{WF}_b(u)&=\overline{\bigcup_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{WF}_b^s(u)}.
	\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The monotonicity of the Sobolev wave-front sets is clear. Also clear is that $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)\supseteq \overline{\bigcup_{s\in\mathbb{R}}\mathsf{WF}_b^s(u)}$. To prove the reverse inclusion, consider a point $(q_0,p^0)\in\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$ and assume it does not belong to the right-hand side. Then, we find a conic neighbourhood of $(q_0,p^0)$ in ${}^{\mathit{b}}\!{T^\ast \overline{M}}$ which does not intersect any $\mathsf{WF}_b^s(u)$. That is, we find a cutoff $\chi$, supported near $q_0$, an $L>0$, and an open cone around $p^0$, both independent of $s$, such that for every $(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\in\Gamma$ we have $\braket{(\xi,\eta)}^s\widehat{\chi u}(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\in L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ for every $s\in\mathbb{R}$. That is, $\chi u\in\mathsf{H}^{\infty,L}$. In view of the analyticity of the Mellin--Fourier transform of $\chi u$, this implies rapid decay in $\Gamma$. That is, $(q_0,p^0)\notin\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
Notice that, when applying the Mellin transform to an element $u\in \mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$, we usually have a pole at 0, corresponding to the fact that these distributions do not necessarily vanish at the boundary (in any reasonable sense). Therefore, we would not have that $\mathcal{M} u$ is square-integrable along $\Im \lambda=0$, as in Lemma 2.1 of \cite{hintz_2016_quasilinear_wave}. For distributions in $\dot\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})\equiv \bigcap_{\alpha}x^\alpha\mathsf{H}_b^{-\infty}(\overline{M})$, our discussion above clarifies why the $b$-wave-front set is essentially independent of the weight, since $x^ \alpha\mathsf{H}^{-\infty}_b\subset x^{\alpha'}\mathsf{H}^{-\infty}_b$ if $\alpha'\leq \alpha$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{theo:b-wave front set and pseudos}
	Let $u\in\mathscr{D}'(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$. Then
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:b-wave-front set with pseudos}
		\mathsf{WF}_b(u)=\bigcap_{\substack{A\in \Psi_b(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})\\Au\in\dot\mathscr{A}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})}}\operatorname{\mathrm{Char}}_b(A).
	\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
The argument is modelled after the proof of the analogous equivalence for the ordinary wave-front set in Appendix A of \cite{shubin2001pseudodifferential}. We denote by $(q_0,p^0)$ a fixed point in the $b$-cotangent bundle.

	We begin by assuming that we have $\widetilde{A}\in \Psi_b^0$ with $\sigma_b(\widetilde{A})(q_0,p^0)\neq 0$ and $\widetilde{A}u\in\dot\mathscr{A}$. First, by a microlocal parametrix construction, we may as well assume that there exist an open set $\widetilde{U}\ni q_0$, lying entirely inside a coordinate patch $\Omega$ over which the $b$-cotangent bundle trivialises, a conic neighbourhood $\widetilde{\Gamma}$ of $p^0$ and an operator ${A}\in \Psi_b^0$ such that the full symbol of $A$ equals 1 in $\widetilde{U}\times \widetilde{\Gamma}$ in the induced coordinates on $\Omega\times \mathbb{R}^n$. Indeed, if $B$ is a microlocal parametrix of $\widetilde{A}$ in any small conic neighbourhood $\widetilde{U}\times \widetilde{\Gamma}$ of $(q_0,p^0)$, then $A=B\widetilde{A}$ has full symbol equal to 1 in $\widetilde{U}\times\widetilde{\Gamma}$.

	Pick now $\chi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$ and $\psi\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ with $\chi\equiv1$ near $q_0$ and $\psi\equiv1$ near $p^0$. We may choose them such that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:support of cutoffs for rapid decay}
		\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} (\chi\psi)\subseteq\{(x,y,\xi,\eta)\colon \sigma_b(A)(x,y,\xi,\eta)=1\}.
	\end{equation}
	It follows that in any coordinate system we have $\psi\chi\sigma_b(A)-\psi\chi\in \mathit{S}^{-\infty}_b$, hence, if $M_\chi$ denotes the operator of multiplication by $\chi$,
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:quantisation of conic cutoff}
		\psi({}^{\mathit{b}}\! D)M_\chi A=\psi({}^{\mathit{b}}\! D)M_\chi\mod{\Psi^{-\infty}_b}.
	\end{equation}
	Since $Au\in\dot\mathscr{A}$, we find using the calculus properties that $\psi({}^{\mathit{b}}\! D)\chi Au\in\dot\mathscr{A}$, so by the above also $\psi({}^{\mathit{b}}\! D)\chi u\in\dot\mathscr{A}$. Applying $\mathcal{M}\operatorname{\mathcal F}$ to it we find then
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:rapid decay in a cone}
		\psi(\xi,\eta)\widehat{\chi u}\quad \text{is rapidly decreasing},
	\end{equation}
	that is, $\widehat{\chi u}$ decreases rapidly in the cone $\Gamma$ around $p^0$. This proves the inclusion $\subseteq$.

	On the other hand, assume we find a conic neighbourhood $\widetilde{U}\times\widetilde{\Gamma}$ of $(q_0,p^0)$ and functions $\chi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\widetilde{U})$, $\chi(q_0)\neq 0$ and $\psi\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\widetilde{\Gamma})$, $\psi(p^0)\neq 0$ and positively 0-homogeneous, such that together they witness the rapid decay of $\psi\widehat{\chi u}$ in $\widetilde{U}\times\widetilde{\Gamma}$. Then, $\widetilde{a}\equiv \chi\psi$ is a Hörmander symbol of order 0. As shown in \cite{hormander1994analysispseudodifferential}, we can find a symbol $a\in\mathit{S}^{0}_{b}$ (see \cite{hintz_2016_quasilinear_wave} for the definition of the class) such that $\widetilde{a}-a\in\mathit{S}^{-\infty}$, in particular we may arrange $a$ to be equal to 1 in a smaller conic neighbourhood $U\times\Gamma$ of $(q_0,p^0)$. Again up to an error in $\mathit{S}^{-\infty}$, we arrange that $A=\operatorname{\mathrm{Op}}_{b}(a)$ is properly supported. Then $A$ is $b$-elliptic at $(q_0,p^0)$, equals $\operatorname{\mathrm{Op}}_{b}(\psi)M_\chi$ up to an error in $\Psi^{-\infty}_b$, and is therefore microlocally the identity in the neighbourhood $U\times\Gamma$. Now, $\widehat{Au}=\psi\widehat{\chi u}+r$, where $r$ is the Mellin--Fourier transform of an element of $\dot\mathscr{A}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$. On the other hand, $Au$ is a compactly supported distribution of extensible type, therefore $\widehat{Au}$ is holomorphic in a half-plane and satisfies the Paley--Wiener bound, in particular is polynomially bounded in $\{(\lambda,\eta)\colon\Im \lambda>K, (\Re\lambda,\eta)\in\Gamma\}$ for some $K$. Moreover, by assumption, it is rapidly decaying along a line $\Im\lambda =L$ with $L>K$ (hence, on all such lines, by \cref{lemma:independence of the line}). Thus, since $\psi=0$ outside $\Gamma$, we find that $\widehat{Au}$ is rapidly decaying there. At the same time, we have rapid decay inside $U\times \Gamma$ by assumption. Thus, $\widehat{Au}$ is rapidly decaying in all directions, which by \cref{theo:paley-wiener for conormal} means that the extensible class of $Au$ belong to $\mathscr{A}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$. That is, $Au\in\dot\mathscr{A}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$. Summing up, $(q_0,p^0)$ does not belong to the $b$-wave-front set of $u$. This shows the reverse inclusion and finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:uniform microlocal cutoff}
	Let $u\in \mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$, $(q_0,p^0)\in{}^{\mathit b}T^{\ast}\overline{M}\setminus O$ and let $W$ be an open conic neighbourhood
	of $(q_0,p^0)$. Then there exist $L>0$ and
	\begin{itemize}
		\item a properly supported $A=\operatorname{\mathrm{Op}}_{la}(a)\in\Psi^0_b(\overline{M})$
		with $\mu\text{-}\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}_b(A)\subset W$ and $a\equiv1$ on an open conic neighbourhood
		$W'\Subset W$ of $(q_0,p^0)$,
		\item a cutoff $\chi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$ with $\chi\equiv1$ near
		$q_0$,
		\item a $0$-homogeneous $\psi$ with $\psi\equiv1$ near $p^0$ and
		$\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}\psi\subset\Gamma$ for some open cone $\Gamma$ around $p^0$,
	\end{itemize}
	such that, if $Au\in\mathscr{A}(\overline{M})$, one has
	\begin{equation*}
		\sup_{(\xi,\eta)\in\Gamma}\braket{(\xi,\eta)}^{N}
		\bigl|\widehat{\chi u}(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\bigr|<\infty
		\qquad\text{for every }N\in\mathbb{N} .
	\end{equation*}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Independently of $u$, choose $A$, $\chi$ and $\psi$ as in the first half of the proof of \cref{theo:b-wave front set and pseudos}, so that $\psi({}^{\mathit{b}}\! D)M_\chi A=\psi({}^{\mathit{b}}\! D)M_\chi$ modulo $\Psi^{-\infty}_b(\overline{M})$. Since $Au\in\mathscr{A}(\overline{M})$, we find $\psi({}^{\mathit{b}}\! D)\chi u\in\mathscr{A}(\overline{M})$, and \cref{theo:paley-wiener for conormal} gives the claimed rapid decay in $\Gamma$. On the other hand, $\mathcal{M} (\chi u)$ is holomorphic in a half-plane, so that by \cref{lemma:independence of the line} its choice is immaterial. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lemma:properties of b-wave-front set}
	If $u\in \mathscr{D}'(\overline{M})$, it holds true:
	\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
		\item $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)=\emptyset$ if, and only if, $u\in\mathscr{A}(\overline{M})$;
		\item If $T\in \operatorname{\mathrm{Diff}}(\overline{M})$ or $T\in \Psi_b(\overline{M})$, then $\mathsf{WF}_b(Tu)\subset \mathsf{WF}_b(u)$;
		\item If $T\in \Psi_b(\overline{M})$, then $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)\subset \mathsf{WF}_b(Tu)\cup \operatorname{\mathrm{Char}}_b(T).$
		\item If $x$ is a boundary-defining function and $T$ is a differential operator of order $m$ with smooth coefficients on $\overline{M}$, then $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)\cap {}^{\mathit b}T^{\ast}_{\partial M}\overline{M}\subset \mathsf{WF}_b(x^mTu)\cup \mathit{T}^{\ast\!}\partial M.$
		\item For $u,v\in\mathscr{D}'(\overline{M})$ we have
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:b-wave-front set of sum}
			\mathsf{WF}_b(u+v)\subset \mathsf{WF}_b(u)\cup\mathsf{WF}_b(v).
		\end{equation}
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Except for the last part, this is part of Theorem 18.3.27 and Proposition 18.3.28 in \cite{hormander1994analysispseudodifferential}. For (e), notice first that $\mathcal{M}\operatorname{\mathcal F}(u+v)$ is holomorphic on a half-plane and that rapid decay on one line propagates to every other line above it by \cref{lemma:independence of the line}. Then, if $\Im \lambda=L_u$ and $\Im\lambda=L_v$ are two lines along which $\mathcal{M}\operatorname{\mathcal F}(u)$ and $\mathcal{M}\operatorname{\mathcal F}(v)$ are respectively rapidly decreasing, we certainly have that both are rapidly decreasing on $\Im\lambda =\max\{L_u,L_v\}$. Thus, if a certain covector does not belong to either $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$ or $\mathsf{WF}_b(v)$, then it also does not belong to $\mathsf{WF}_b(u+v)$. This finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
		\item In view of \cref{lemma:conormal+dual-conormal=smooth}, (a) above can be improved if we know $u\in\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$: it suffices to look at the characteristic sets of $A\in \Psi_b(\overline{M})$ such that $Au\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M})$, and therefore $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)=\emptyset$ if, and only if, $u\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M})$. This is the case, for example, if $Pu=0$ for some non-characteristic differential operator on $\overline{M}$, see \cref{cor:kernel of NHO is normally regular} below.
		\item Point (d) in \cref{lemma:properties of b-wave-front set} appears discouraging at first sight, since it seems that we cannot control the direction of singularities of solutions of differential equations along $\partial M$. However, notice that it does not take any boundary conditions into account. We will give a vast improvement over it in a moment.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lemma:extensible=supported for dual-conormal}
	We have
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:dual-conormal meets no boundary distribution}
		\dot\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})\cap \dot\mathscr{D}'_{\partial M}(\overline{M})=\{0\}.
	\end{equation}
	Consequently, the restriction map of
	\eqref{eq:exact sequence for supported/extensible distributions} restricts to a
	bijection $\dot\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})\xrightarrow{\ \cdot|_{M}\ }\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$ (cf. \cite{alvarez_lopez_topology_2024}). Finally, if $u\in\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$ and $U\in\dot\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$ denotes the corresponding	supported representative, then
	\begin{equation*}
		\mathsf{WF}_b(u)=\mathsf{WF}_b(U).
	\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The first part is shown in Chapter I, Section 3 of \cite{melrose1982transformationofboundaryproblems}, in the discussion preceding Proposition 3.28.

	Consider the restriction map in \eqref{eq:exact sequence for supported/extensible distributions}. After \cite{alvarez_lopez_topology_2024}, we show that it restricts to a bijection between $\dot\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$ and $\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$. The injectivity is clear: if $U_1, U_2\in\dot\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$ are supported distributions restricting to the same $u\in\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$, then $U_1-U_2\in \dot\mathscr{D}'_{\partial M}(\overline{M})$, so that, by \eqref{eq:dual-conormal meets no boundary distribution}, it has to vanish. For the surjectivity, notice that any test function on $\overline{M}$ is automatically supported conormal to $\partial M$, with continuous embedding. Indeed, in adapted coordinates, the seminorms of $\dot\mathscr{A}$ are the $L^\infty$-norms of $(x\partial_x)^k\partial^\alpha_y \varphi$, which are clearly controlled by a finite number of $\mathit C^{\infty}_c$-seminorms. By definition, the pairing $\braket{u,\varphi}$ of $u\in\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$ with $\varphi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$ is then well-defined. It follows that every $u\in\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$ has a \textit{canonical} supported representative which is itself dual-conormal.

	Finally, notice that $x^{-\mathrm{i}\lambda-1}e^{-\mathrm{i} y\eta}$ is a conormal distribution. Therefore, both $u\in\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$ and its canonical representative $U\in\dot\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$ can be paired with it. Clearly, $\widehat{\chi U}=\widehat{\chi u}$ then, which concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:normally regular distributions}
	A distribution $u\in\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$ is \textit{normally regular}, written $u\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$, if $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)\subset T^\ast M\cup \mathit{T}^{\ast\!}\partial{M}$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{example:A' vs N'}
	Consider the supported distribution $u=\sum_{j\geq 1}e^{-j^2}\delta_{1/j}$ on $[0,\infty)$. That this pairs continuously with $\varphi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c([0,\infty))$ can be seen directly: clearly the sum converges since we can estimate it by $\|\varphi\|_{L^\infty}\sum e^{-j^2}$, moreover the pairing can be controlled by the $L^\infty$ norm of any finite number of derivatives (after Taylor expansion). Then, $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u=\operatorname{\mathrm{singsupp}} u=\{0\}\cup\{1/j,j\in\mathbb{N}\}$, so $u$ is not a smooth function of $x$. On the other hand, after Mellin transforming $u$ we obtain
	\begin{equation*}
		|\braket{u,x^{-\mathrm{i}\lambda-1}}|\leq \sum_{j\geq 1}e^{-j^2}e^{(1-\Im\lambda)\log j},
	\end{equation*}
	which is bounded on any strip $|\Im\lambda|\leq L$. Therefore, according to \cref{theo:paley-wiener for dual-conormal}, $u\in\mathscr{A}'([0,\infty))$.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{theo:smoothness and solvability in N'}
	Let $u\in\mathscr{D}'(\overline{M})$. Then
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item we have $u\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ if, and only if, there exists an open set $U\subset\overline{M}$, an $\varepsilon>0$ and a boundary-defining function $x$ with $U\simeq\partial M\times[0,\varepsilon)_x$, such that in local coordinates we have \[u\in\mathit C^{\infty}([0,\varepsilon);\mathscr{D}'(U\cap\partial M)),\]
		the latter meaning by definition that $\braket{u,\varphi}$ is a smooth function of $x$ for every $\varphi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\partial M)$;
		\item if $u\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ then for all $A\in \Psi_b(\overline{M})$ or $A\in\operatorname{\mathrm{Diff}}(\overline{M})$ we have $Au\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$;
		\item if $Pu=f\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ and $\partial M$ is non-characteristic for $P$, then $u\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:kernel of NHO is normally regular}
	For $P\in\operatorname{\mathrm{Diff}}(\overline{M})$ with non-characteristic $\partial M$ we have $\ker(P\colon \mathscr{D}'(\overline{M})\to\mathscr{D}'(\overline{M}))\subset\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:restriction and boundary WF set}
	Any $u\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ has traces of all orders at $\partial M$, i.e. for every $k\in\mathbb{N}$, $\partial^k_{\nu} u$ exists as an element of $\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ and restricts to $\partial M$ to give an element of $\mathcal D'(\overline{M})$. Moreover, $\mathsf{WF}(\gamma_0 \partial^k_\nu u)\subset\partial\mathsf{WF}(u)$.
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:LS-condition and joint characteristic set}
	Let $(P,\gamma_0 B)$ be a boundary-value problem on the manifold with boundary $\overline{M}$ (that is, $P, B$ are differential operators with smooth coefficients on $\overline{M}$ and $\gamma_0$ is the restriction map to the boundary). Let $(y,\zeta)\in T^\ast_{\partial M}\overline{M}$ with $\zeta$ not proportional to the interior conormal $\nu_{(0,y)}$. We say that the boundary-value problem satisfies the Lopatinskij--Shapiro condition at $(y,\zeta)$ (or that the boundary-value problem is \textit{elliptic} at $(y,\zeta)$) if the map
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lopatinskij--Shapiro map}
		\operatorname{\mathrm{LS}}_{y,\zeta}\colon X^+_{y,\zeta}\ni u\mapsto b(y,\zeta+D_s\nu_{(0,y)})u|_{s=0}\in \mathbb{C}
	\end{equation}
	is bijective. We introduce then the \textit{boundary characteristic set} of the pair $(P,\gamma_0B)$ as the subset $\operatorname{\mathrm{Char}}(P;B)$ of $T^\ast \partial M$ where either \eqref{eq:Lopatinskij--Shapiro map} is not bijective or the point $(y,\zeta)$ has a preimage under $\varrho^t$ that is characteristic for $P$. Explicitly,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:joint characteristic set}
		\operatorname{\mathrm{Char}}(P;B):=\{(y,\eta)\in T^\ast \partial M\colon (\exists \zeta\in T^\ast_y \overline{M}, \varrho^t(\zeta)=\eta, p(y,\zeta)=0)\text{ or }(\ker\operatorname{\mathrm{LS}}_{y,\zeta}\neq \{0\})\}.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{theo:b-WF with elliptic boundary conditions}
	If $P$ is a differential operator on the manifold $\overline{M}$ with non-characteristic boundary $\partial M$, $\gamma_0B$ is a local boundary condition for $P$, and $u\in \mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ is a solution of the homogeneous boundary problem $(P, \gamma_0B)u=0$, then we have
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:localisation of singularities with boundary conditions}
		\mathsf{WF}_b(u)\subset\operatorname{\mathrm{Char}} (P)\dot\cup \operatorname{\mathrm{Char}}(P;B).
	\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{theo:DBC satisfies LS}
	Let $u\in \mathscr{N}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+})$ satisfy $\Box u\equiv(\partial^2_t+\Delta_{x,y}) u=0$ and $u|_{x=0}=0$, where $\Delta_{x,y}$ is $-\partial^2_{xx}-\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\partial^2_{y^j y^j}$. We have $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)|_{x=0}=\partial\mathsf{WF}(u)\subset \{(t,0,y,\tau,0,\eta)\colon \tau^2\geq |\eta|^2\}$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
By \cref{theo:b-WF with elliptic boundary conditions} we know $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)\subset\operatorname{\mathrm{Char}}(\Box;\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}})$, so that we need to compute the joint characteristic set. To this end, we analyse in which directions the boundary-value problem $(\Box,\gamma_0)$ satisfies the Lopatinskij--Shapiro condition at a generic point $q\in \partial \overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+}=\{(t,0,y)\}$.

	The space $X^+_{q,(\tau,\xi,\eta)}$ is determined by finding the bounded solutions to the ODE $(\tau^2-(\xi+D_s)^2-|\eta|^2)u=0$, that is,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:ODE for LS condition}
		\partial_s^2 u+2\mathrm{i} \xi \partial_su-(\xi^2+|\eta|^2-\tau^2)u=0.
	\end{equation}
	One calculates the discriminant to be $4(|\eta|^2-\tau^2)$, and analyses separately the cases:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\tau^2< |\eta|^2$, in which case we have the solutions $e^{-s(\mathrm{i}\xi\pm\sqrt{|\eta|^2-\tau^2})}$;
		\item $\tau^2=|\eta|^2$, in which case the solutions are $e^{-\mathrm{i} s\xi}$ and $s e^{-\mathrm{i} s\xi}$;
		\item $\tau^2>|\eta|^2$, in which case we have the solutions $e^{-\mathrm{i} s (\xi+\sqrt{\tau^2-|\eta|^2})}$ and $e^{-\mathrm{i} s(\xi-\sqrt{\tau^2-|\eta|^2})}$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Therefore, the space $X^+_{q,(\tau,0,\eta)}$ is, in the three cases above, the span of
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $e^{-s(\mathrm{i} \xi+\sqrt{|\eta|^2-\tau^2})}$ if $\tau^2<|\eta|^2$;
		\item $e^{-\mathrm{i}\xi s}$ if $\tau^2=|\eta|^2$;
		\item $e^{-\mathrm{i} s(\xi\pm\sqrt{\tau^2-|\eta|^2})}$ if $\tau^2>|\eta|^2$.
	\end{enumerate}
	The map $\operatorname{\mathrm{LS}}_{q,(\tau,\xi,\eta)}$ is, for $B=\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}$, just evaluation at $s=0$, so that, if $(\tau,\eta)\neq 0$ (that is, the covector $(\tau,\xi,\eta)$ is not proportional to $\nu_q$), $\operatorname{\mathrm{LS}}_{q,(\tau,\xi,\eta)}$ is a bijection in the first two cases. In the third case, we have a nontrivial kernel of $\operatorname{\mathrm{LS}}$. However, the third region is also the image via the transpose of the anchor map $\varrho^t$ of $\{(q,(\tau,\xi,\eta))\colon -\tau^2+\xi^2+|\eta|^2=0\}$, the characteristic set of $\Box$. That is, the covectors in the third region are tangent covectors to the boundary having a characteristic preimage for $P$, lying by definition in $\operatorname{\mathrm{Char}}(\Box;\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}})$. Of course, the covectors with $\tau^2=|\eta|^2$ are characteristic for $P$ too, when viewed as elements of $T^\ast \overline{M}$. Therefore, we have determined the joint characteristic set to be the region
	\begin{equation}
		\operatorname{\mathrm{Char}}(\Box;\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}})=\{(q,(\tau,\eta))\in T^\ast \partial M\colon \tau^2\geq |\eta|^2 \},
	\end{equation}
	which concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
After we have introduced the necessary geometric preliminaries in \cref{sect:GHSTB and IBVP}, \cref{theo:DBC satisfies LS} will say that the singularities of elements of the kernel of a normally hyperbolic operator are, at boundary points, constrained to the \textit{compressed causal cone} (see \cref{def:causal compressed b-covectors} for the definition).
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:b-HS-valued distributions}
	Let $\overline{M}$ be a smooth manifold with boundary. A \textit{supported $\mathcal H$-valued distribution}, $u\in\dot\mathscr{D}'(\overline{M};\mathcal H)$ is a weakly continuous linear form $u\colon\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})\to\mathcal H$, that is, for every $h\in \mathcal H$ the linear form $(h,u(\cdot))$ is in $\dot\mathscr{D}'(\overline{M})$. An \textit{extensible $\mathcal H$-valued distribution}, $u\in\mathscr{D}'(\overline{M};\mathcal H)$, is a weakly continuous linear map $u\colon\dot{\mathit C}^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})\to\mathcal H$. The notation $\mathscr{F}(\overline{M};\mathcal H)$ shall be used for any other space of distributions introduced in \cref{sect:distributions on manifolds with boundary} to denote the obvious generalisation.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:b-wave-front set of hilbert-valued distribution}
	Let $u\in\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M};\mathcal H)$. We say that $(x_0,y_0,\xi_0,\eta_0)\in{}^{\mathit{b}}\!\mathit{T}^{\ast\!}\overline{M}$ does not belong to $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$ (or that it is $b$-regular directed) if there exist a chart $\varkappa\colon U\to \overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+}$ near $(x_0,y_0)$, a cutoff $\chi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$ with $\chi\equiv1$ near $(x_0,y_0)$, a conic neighbourhood $\Gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ of $(\xi_0,\eta_0)$ and $L>0$ such that $\mathcal{M} (\chi u)(\lambda)$ is holomorphic in a neighbourhood of the line $\{\Im\lambda=L \}$ and, for all $(\Re\lambda,\eta)\in \Gamma$ and all $N\in\mathbb{N}$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:rapid decay in a cone for HS-valued distribution}
		\|\widehat{\varkappa_\ast(\chi u)}(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\|\lesssim \braket{(\xi,\eta)}^{-N}.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:properties of b-WF for HS-distributions}
	Let $X$ be a smooth domain in $\overline{\mathbb{R}^n_+}$ and let $u\in\mathscr{A}'( X;\mathcal H)$. Then:
	\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
		\item If $u$ satisfies \eqref{eq:rapid decay in a cone for HS-valued distribution} for some $\chi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c({X})$, then it also satisfies it for $f\chi$ for all $f\in\mathit C^{\infty}({X})$. In particular, $\mathsf{WF}_b(fu)\subset\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$.
		\item If $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u$ is compact, then $\widehat{u}$ is smooth and polynomially bounded in the norm: there exist constants $C>0,m\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:cptly suppd HS-valued has polynomially bdd FM transform}
			\|\widehat{u}(\xi,\eta)\|\leq C\braket{(\xi,\eta)}^m.
		\end{equation}
		\item If $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)=\emptyset$, then $u\in\mathit C^{\infty}({X};\mathcal H)$.
		\item Let $w\in \mathscr{A}'( X\times X)$ be defined by $w(f,g)=\left({u(\overline{f})}, u(g)\right)$. Then, denoting by $z=(x,y)$, $\zeta=(\xi,\eta)$ the canonical coordinates on ${}^{\mathit{b}}\!\mathit{T}^{\ast\!} X$,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:wave-front set of bidistribution vs distribution}
			(z,\zeta)\in\mathsf{WF}_b(u)\iff ((z,-\zeta),(z,\zeta))\in \mathsf{WF}_b(w),
		\end{equation}
		and moreover if $\zeta_0\neq 0$ and $(z_0,\zeta_0)$ does not belong to $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$, then for any $(z,\zeta)$ neither $((z_0,-\zeta_0),(z,\zeta))$ nor $((z,\zeta),(z_0,\zeta_0))$ belong to $\mathsf{WF}_b(w)$.
		\item $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$ transforms as a subset of the $b$-cotangent bundle.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
		\item This is proven in the same way as for the ordinary wave-front set of ordinary distributions.

		\item That $\widehat{u}$ is smooth follows by integration by parts using the standard argument for compactly supported distributions. For the bound, notice that, by definition, $u$ can be paired with $x^{-\mathrm{i}\lambda-1}e^{-\mathrm{i} y\eta}$. By continuity of $u$ on $\dot\mathscr{A}(\overline{X};\mathcal H)$, we find that for all compact $K\supset\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u$ and all $s\in\mathbb{R}$ there exist constants $C>0$, $k\in\mathbb{N}$ such that
		\begin{align*}
			\|u(x^{-\mathrm{i}\lambda-1}e^{-\mathrm{i} y\eta})\|&\leq C\sum_{j=0}^k\left\|(x\partial_x)^j\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k-j}\partial^\alpha_y (x^{-\mathrm{i}\lambda-1}e^{-\mathrm{i} y\eta})\right\|_{\mathsf{H}^s}\\
			&\leq C\sum_{j=0}^k\left\|(-\mathrm{i}\lambda-1)^j\sum_{|\alpha|\leq k-j}(-\mathrm{i}\eta)^\alpha e^{-\mathrm{i} y\eta}x^{-\mathrm{i}\lambda-1}\right\|_{\mathsf{H}^s}\\
			&\leq \widetilde{C}(1+|(\lambda,\eta)|)^k,
		\end{align*}
		where $\widetilde{C}$ is a sufficiently large positive constant.

		\item If $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)=\emptyset$, then for every point $(x,y)\in{X}$ and every covector $(\xi,\eta)\in{}^{\mathit b}T^{\ast}_{(x,y)}X$ we find $f\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c({X})$, $f(x,y)=1$, such that $\|\widehat{fu}(\lambda,\eta)\|$ is rapidly decreasing in a cone around $(\xi,\eta)$ in $\braket{(\Re\lambda,\eta)}$. By compactness of the $b$-cosphere bundle we find a single cutoff $\chi$, depending on $(x,y)$ but not on $(\xi,\eta)$, such that $\widehat{\chi u}$ is rapidly decreasing in all directions. Since $\chi u\in\mathscr{E}'(X)$, the Mellin--Fourier transform is holomorphic in a half-plane and satisfies there the Paley--Wiener bound
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:paley-wiener bound for HS-valued}
			\|\widehat{\chi u}(\lambda, \eta)\|\leq Ce^{A|\Im\lambda|}(1+|\Re\lambda|)^s.
		\end{equation}
		This means that $\chi u$ is actually a conormal distribution to $X\cap\partial \mathbb{R}^n_+$, see \cref{theo:paley-wiener for conormal}. Since $u\in\mathscr{A}'({X};\mathcal H)$ by assumption, we have $u\in\mathit C^{\infty}({X};\mathcal H)$ in view of \cref{lemma:conormal+dual-conormal=smooth}.

		\item It is no restriction to assume that $w$ has compact support, since we can always localise $u$. That $w\in\mathscr{A}'(X\times X)$ follows then by Mellin transform: we have that $\mathcal{M} w(\overline{\lambda_1},\lambda_2)=\left(u(x_1^{\mathrm{i}\overline{\lambda_1}-1}),u(x_2^{-\mathrm{i}\lambda_2-1})\right)$, with values in $\mathscr{D}'(\mathbb{R}^{2(n-1)})$, is holomorphic in the product $\{\Im\lambda_1>0\}\times\{\Im\lambda_2>0\}$ (recall that $(\cdot,\cdot)$ is conjugate-linear in the first slot). After being regularised by $\prod_{j=0}^{\lfloor L\rfloor}(\lambda_1+\mathrm{i} j)(\lambda_2+\mathrm{i} j)$, $w$ is polynomially bounded in $|\Im \lambda_1|,|\Im \lambda_2|\leq L$, since this is true for $u$. By \cref{theo:mellin transform of A'} applied to distributions in $X\times X$ we find $w\in\mathscr{A}'(X\times X)$.

		Now assume $\zeta =(\xi,\eta)$ and $(z,-\zeta,z,\zeta)\notin\mathsf{WF}_b(w)$, so that we find $L>0$ and a function $f\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c({X}\times X)$ with $\widehat{fw}(-\xi+\mathrm{i} L,-\eta,\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)$ rapidly decreasing in a conic neighbourhood $\Gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^{2n}_0$ of $(z,-\zeta,z,\zeta)$. We may choose $f=f_1\otimes f_1$ for some positive function $f_1\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(X)$, from which it follows
		\begin{equation*}\label{eq:rapid decay of M-F transform of u from decay of w}
			\|\widehat{f_1 u}(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\|^2=|\widehat{(f_1\!\otimes\! f_1)w}(-\xi+\mathrm{i} L,-\eta,\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)|\lesssim \braket{\zeta}^{-N}.
		\end{equation*}
		That is, $(z,\zeta)$ is not in $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$. On the other hand, suppose $(z_0,\zeta_0)\notin\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$, so that for an $L>0$ and an $f\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c({X})$ we have rapid decay of $\widehat{fu}(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)$ for $(\xi,\eta)$ in a conic neighbourhood $\Gamma$ of $(z_0,\zeta_0)$. By Cauchy--Schwarz
		\begin{equation*}\label{eq:rapid decay of M-F transform of w given that of u}
			|\widehat{(g\otimes f)w}(\xi_1+\mathrm{i} L,\eta_1,\xi_2+\mathrm{i} L,\eta_2)|\leq \|u(\overline{g}x_1^{+\mathrm{i}\xi_1-1+L}e^{\mathrm{i} y\eta_1})\|\cdot\|u(fx_2^{-\mathrm{i}\xi_2-1+L}e^{-\mathrm{i} y\eta_2})\|,
		\end{equation*}
		where the second factor is rapidly decreasing for $(\xi_2,\eta_2)\in \Gamma$. Since, for every $g\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{X})$, the first factor is polynomially bounded in the region where it is holomorphic, it follows that $(z,\zeta,z_0,\zeta_0)\notin\mathsf{WF}_b(w)$ for any $(z,\zeta)\in{}^{\mathit{b}}\!\mathit{T}^{\ast\!} {X}$. The same proof, exchanging the roles of $f$ and $g$, gives that $(z_0,-\zeta_0,z,\zeta)\notin\mathsf{WF}_b(w)$.

		\item This follows from the previous point.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
After we introduce the setup of quantum field theory on curved spacetimes in \cref{sect:qft}, part (d) of the previous result will relate the $b$-wave-front set of the two-point function $\omega_2$ ($w$ from above) to that of the one-particle distribution $\Phi$ ($u$ in the Proposition).
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{theo:weak and strong b-wave-front set}
	For any $u\in\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M};\mathcal H)$, let $u_v\in\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$ be defined by $\braket{u_v,\varphi}\equiv (v,\braket{u,\varphi})$ for all $\varphi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$. Then
	\begin{equation}
		\mathsf{WF}_b(u)=\overline{\bigcup_{v\in \mathcal H}\mathsf{WF}_b(u_v)}.
	\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
It suffices to prove the statement locally. Also recall that, according to \cref{lemma:properties of b-wave-front set}, if $u\in\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$ we have $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)=\emptyset$ if, and only if, $u$ is $\mathit C^{\infty}$ in the norm topology, and that $\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})\subset\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$. By nuclearity, the same is true for $\mathcal H$-valued objects.

	Thus, if $(q_0,p^0)\notin\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$, meaning that we find an open cone $\Gamma$ and a cutoff $\chi$ with $\chi(q_0)\neq 0$ such that $\widehat{\chi u}$ is rapidly decreasing in $\Gamma$, then, by Cauchy--Schwarz, each $\widehat{\chi u_v}$ decays rapidly in the same cone $\Gamma$. That is, $(q_0,p^0)\notin\mathsf{WF}_b(u_v)$. Since both sets are closed, we find $(q_0,p^0)\notin \overline{\bigcup_{v\in \mathcal H}\mathsf{WF}_b(u_v)}$.

	Conversely, let $(q_0,p^0)\notin \overline{\bigcup_{v\in\mathcal H}\mathsf{WF}_b(u_v)}$. Then, there exists an open conic neighbourhood $W\subset{}^{\mathit b}T^{\ast}\overline{M}\setminus O$ with
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:common regular region}
		W\cap\mathsf{WF}_b(u_v)=\emptyset\quad\text{for every }v\in\mathcal H.
	\end{equation}
	Let $\chi$, $\psi$, $\Gamma$ and $L$ be as given by \cref{cor:uniform microlocal cutoff} and thus independent of $v$. Then we have
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform rapid decay}
		\sup_{(\xi,\eta)\in\Gamma}\braket{(\xi,\eta)}^{N}
		\bigl|\widehat{\chi u_v}(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\bigr|<\infty
		\quad \forall N\in\mathbb{N},\, \forall v\in\mathcal H.
	\end{equation}

	Fix then $N\in\mathbb{N}$. The Mellin--Fourier transform $\widehat{\chi u}(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)$ is an element of $\mathcal H$ by definition, and for $(\xi,\eta)\in\Gamma$ we consider the conjugate-linear functionals
	\begin{equation*}
		T_{\xi,\eta}\colon\mathcal H\to\mathbb{C},\qquad
		T_{\xi,\eta}(v)\equiv\braket{(\xi,\eta)}^{N}\,\widehat{\chi u_v}(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)
		=\left(v,\braket{(\xi,\eta)}^{N}\widehat{\chi u}(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\right).
	\end{equation*}
	Each $T_{\xi,\eta}$ is bounded, with $\|T_{\xi,\eta}\|=\braket{(\xi,\eta)}^{N} \|\widehat{\chi u}(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\|$ as can be easily seen with the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality. That is, the family $\{T_{\xi,\eta}\}_{(\xi,\eta)\in\Gamma}$ is pointwise bounded. By Banach--Steinhaus, it is uniformly bounded as well, that is, we find $C_N>0$ with
	\begin{equation*}
		\bigl\|\widehat{\chi u}(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\bigr\|\leq C_N\braket{(\xi,\eta)}^{-N},
		\qquad(\xi,\eta)\in\Gamma.
	\end{equation*}
	As $N\in\mathbb{N}$ was arbitrary, $(q_0,p^0)\notin\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$, which is the required inclusion.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:HS-valued N' is preserved}
	If $u\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M};\mathcal H)$ and either $A\in \Psi_b(\overline{M})$ or $A\in \operatorname{\mathrm{Diff}}(\overline{M})$, then $Au\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M};\mathcal H)$. Similarly, if $\partial M$ is non-characteristic for $P\in\operatorname{\mathrm{Diff}}(\overline{M})$ and $u\in \mathscr{D}'(\overline{M};\mathcal H)$ satisfies $Pu\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M};\mathcal H)$, then $u\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M};\mathcal H)$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Neither $\Psi_b(\overline{M})$ nor $\operatorname{\mathrm{Diff}}(\overline{M})$ enlarge $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$ for any scalar extensible distribution $u$ on $\overline{M}$. For $u\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M};\mathcal H)$ and any $v\in\mathcal H$ we have the scalar distribution $u_v=(v,u(\cdot))$, which is in $\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ by definition and has then $\partial\mathsf{WF}(u_v)\subset T^\ast\partial M$. Then $Au_v=(Au)_v\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ by \cref{theo:smoothness and solvability in N'} (2), so that by \cref{theo:weak and strong b-wave-front set} we find $\partial\mathsf{WF}(Au)\subset T^\ast\partial M$, i.e. $Au\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M};\mathcal H)$. For the second statement, the proof is the same using \cref{theo:smoothness and solvability in N'} (3).
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:GHSTB}
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item A \textit{spacetime with timelike boundary} is an oriented and time-oriented Lorentzian manifold $\overline{M}$, having a boundary $\partial M$, embedded into $\overline{M}$ as a timelike hypersurface (that is, the normal vector field to $\partial M$ is everywhere spacelike). In particular, the boundary is itself an oriented time-oriented Lorentzian manifold.
		\item If $\overline{M}$ is a spacetime with timelike boundary and $p, q\in \overline{M}$, one says that $q$ belongs to the \textit{chronological} (resp.\ \textit{causal}) future of $p$, $I^+(p)$ (resp.\ $J^+(p)$), if $p$ can be joined to $q$ by a future-directed timelike (resp.\ causal) $\mathsf{H}^1$-curve (see \cref{rem:causality and H1-curves}). One denotes by $I^+(K)$ (resp.\ $J^+(K)$) the union of the chronological (resp.\ causal) futures of all points in the set $K\subset \overline{M}$. The same definitions with roles reversed define the chronological and causal past of $q$, namely the sets $I^-(q)$ and $J^-(q)$.
		\item One calls a spacetime with timelike boundary \textit{causal} if there are no closed future-directed causal curves and \textit{globally hyperbolic} if it is causal and for any $p,q\in \overline{M}$ the sets $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ are compact.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{rem:causality and H1-curves}
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item The standard definitions of timelike/lightlike/spacelike/causal vectors and submanifolds carry over to this setting without change.
		\item The definition of $J^{\pm} (p)$ uses the notion of $\mathsf{H}^1$-curves, namely curves whose local parametrisations are in the Sobolev space $\mathsf{H}^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R})$. On the one hand, this ensures that some desirable generalisations of properties of the boundaryless case, like the existence of Cauchy surfaces, remain true. On the other hand, a maximally extended causal curve on $\overline{M}$ will not be smooth in general, since it can hit the timelike boundary and be reflected. To define $I^+(p)$, we can as well use smooth curves.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- prop-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:properties of ghstb}
	Let $\overline{M}$ be a globally hyperbolic spacetime with timelike boundary. Then
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $\overline{M}$ admits a \textit{Cauchy temporal function}, namely a function $t\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M})$ with future-directed timelike gradient whose level sets are spacelike hypersurfaces which are intersected exactly once by any inextensible causal $\mathsf{H}^1$-curve (i.e. Cauchy surfaces). In addition, $t$ can be chosen such that $\nabla t$ is tangent to $\partial M$.
		\item $\partial M$ is a globally hyperbolic spacetime (without boundary), and we can choose the restriction of $t$ as a Cauchy temporal function on it.
		\item $M$ is a smooth causal spacetime, and we can choose the restriction of $t$ as a temporal function on it.
		\item $\overline{M}$ is isometric to $\mathbb{R}\times \overline{\Sigma}$ with a metric $g=\beta\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t^2-g_t$, where $\overline{\Sigma}$ is a Riemannian manifold with boundary, $\beta\colon\mathbb{R}\times\overline{\Sigma}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is a positive function and $g_t$ is a smooth family of Riemannian metrics on $\overline{\Sigma}$. Any slice $\overline{\Sigma}_a=t^{-1}(a)$ is a Cauchy surface. Correspondingly, $\partial M\cong \mathbb{R}\times\partial \Sigma$ and $M\cong\mathbb{R}\times\Sigma$ with the restricted metrics.
		\item The previous property and the existence of a Cauchy surface (with boundary) are both equivalent to global hyperbolicity.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end prop-3 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:past and future compact}
	Let $\overline{M}$ be a globally hyperbolic spacetime with timelike boundary. For $K\subset\overline{M}$ we write $J(K):=J^+(K)\cup J^-(K)$.
	A subset $A\subset\overline{M}$ is called
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item \textit{spatially compact} if there exists a compact set $K\subset\overline{M}$
		such that $A\subset J(K)$;
		\item \textit{past-compact} resp.\ \textit{future-compact} if $A\cap J^-(K)$ resp.\
		$A\cap J^+(K)$ is compact for every compact set $K\subset\overline{M}$;
		\item \textit{strictly past-compact} resp.\ \textit{strictly future-compact} if there
		exists a compact set $K\subset\overline{M}$ such that $A\subset J^+(K)$ resp.\
		$A\subset J^-(K)$.
	\end{enumerate}
	A distribution $u\in\dot{\mathscr{D}}'(\overline{M})$ is called spatially compact, (strictly)
	past-compact, or (strictly) future-compact if its support $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u$ has the
	corresponding property. If $\mathscr{F}$ is a space of distributions on $\overline{M}$, we
	denote by $\mathscr{F}_{\mathrm{sc}}$, $\mathscr{F}_{\mathrm{pc}/\mathrm{fc}}$ and
	$\mathscr{F}_{\mathrm{spc}/\mathrm{sfc}}$ the subspaces of those elements of $\mathscr{F}$ which are
	spatially compact, past-/future-compact, and strictly past-/future-compact.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{theo:existence and uniqueness}
	Assume $\overline{M}$ is spatially compact. If $f\in \mathsf{H}^s_{\mathrm{loc},\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$ and $v\in\mathsf{H}^{s+1}_{\mathrm{loc},\mathrm{pc}}(\partial M)$, there exists a unique $u\in\mathsf{H}^{s+1}_{\mathrm{loc},\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$ that solves \eqref{eq:retarded BVP}.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:smooth existence}
	If $f\in \mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$ and $v\in \mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\partial M)$, then there exists a unique $u\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$ satisfying $Pu=f$ in ${M}$ and $u|_{\partial M}=v$. Moreover, the assignment $(f,v)\mapsto u$ is continuous.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The existence is an immediate consequence of \cref{theo:existence and uniqueness}, using that $\bigcap_s\mathsf{H}^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(\overline{M})=\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M})$ and $\bigcap_s\mathsf{H}^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(\partial M)=\mathit C^{\infty}(\partial M)$. The continuity follows since the topology of $\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M})$ can be defined using $\mathsf{H}^s$-norms for large $s$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{theo:propagators}
	Let $\overline{M}$ be a globally hyperbolic spacetime with timelike boundary. For every $f\in\mathit C^{\infty}_\mathrm{pc}(\overline{M}), v\in\mathit C^{\infty}_\mathrm{pc}(\partial M)$ we find a unique $u\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$ such that $Pu=f$ and $u|_{\partial M}=v$. Moreover, we have
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:support of retarded solution}
		\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u\subset J^+(\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} f\cup \operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} v).
	\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
We have
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item If $\beta$ is future-directed timelike and $\alpha$ is future-directed causal, then $T_\zeta(\alpha,\beta)$ is positive semidefinite, and positive definite exactly if $\alpha$ is timelike.
		\item Same as (1) but with $\alpha,\beta$ past-directed.
		\item If $T_\cdot(\alpha,\beta)$ is positive definite, then $\alpha, \beta$ are necessarily timelike and in the same connected component of the causal cone.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The only addition with respect to the reference is the statement about the positive semidefinite case. This is a quick consequence: since $T_\zeta(\cdot,\beta)$ is linear, the set
	\begin{equation*}
		\{\alpha\in T^\ast_z\overline{M}\colon T_\zeta(\alpha,\beta)\ge 0\}
	\end{equation*}
	is a closed cone, containing the future-directed timelike directions in view of the statement for future-directed timelike covectors. Since the future causal cone is the closure of the future chronological cone, the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lemma:stress-energy tensor for conormal direction}
	Let $z\in\partial M$, $U$ a neighbourhood of $z$ in $\overline{M}$ and $\nu_z$a (spacelike) exterior conormal covector to $\partial M$. Let $u\in C^1(U)$ be such that $u|_{\partial M\cap U}=0$ so that $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u_z=\sigma\nu_z$ for some $\sigma\in\mathbb{C}$. Then, if $L=\beta^\sharp$ (with respect to $g$),
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:stress-energy tensor for conormal direction}
		T_{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u}(\nu_z,\beta)=|\sigma|^2p(\nu_z,\nu_z)\braket{\nu_z,L}.
	\end{equation}
	In particular, if $\sigma\neq 0$, then $T_{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u}(\nu_z,\beta)\ge 0$ if, and only if, $L$ does not point outward from $\overline{M}$, with equality precisely for $L$ tangent to $\partial M$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
For any $\sigma\in\mathbb{C}$, a direct computation with $\zeta=\sigma \nu_z$ shows that
	\begin{equation*}
		T_{\sigma\nu_z}(\nu_z,\beta)=|\sigma|^2p(\nu_z,\nu_z)p(\nu_z,\beta)=|\sigma|^2p(\nu_z,\nu_z)\braket{\nu_z,L},
	\end{equation*}
	where $L=\beta^\sharp$. With this formula, the rest of the proof is quick: if $L$ is tangent to $\partial M$, then $\braket{\nu_z,L}=0$, and since $p(\nu_z,\nu_z)<0$ we have that the sign of $T$ is positive exactly when $L$ points inward. This finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lemma:divergence of SE current}
	For every $u\in C^2(\overline{M})$ there exists a complex quadratic form $R$ in $(u,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u)$, with coefficients depending only on $\nabla L$ and on the potential $V$, such that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:divergence of SE tensor}
		\operatorname{\mathrm{div}} \mathcal J[u]=2\Re\left(\overline{\braket{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u,L}}Pu\right)+R(u,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u).
	\end{equation}
	Moreover, $R$ is continuous and for any compact $K\subset\overline{M}$ there is $C_K>0$ such that
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:bounded quadratic remainder}
		|R(u,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u)|\leq C_K(|u|^2+|\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u|^2).
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lemma:slab-cone is a Lipschitz domain}
	Consider the metric splitting $\overline{M}\simeq\mathbb{R}_t\times\overline{\Sigma}$, let $z\in\overline{M}$ and let $a<b$ be real numbers. Then $J^-(z)\cap t^{-1}[a,b]$ is a Lipschitz domain in $\overline{M}$, irrespective of whether it intersects $\partial M$ and of the value of $t(z)$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{theo:support of solutions}
	Let $f\in\mathit C^{\infty}_\mathrm{pc}(\overline{M})$, $v\in\mathit C^{\infty}_\mathrm{pc}(\partial M)$. Assume that $u\in\mathit C^{\infty}_\mathrm{pc}(\overline{M})$ solves $Pu=f$ on $M$ and $\gamma_0u=v$ on $\partial M$. Then,
	\begin{equation}
		\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u\subset J^+(\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} f\cup\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} v).
	\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Let $K\equiv \operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} f\cup \operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} v$ and fix $z\notin J^+(K)$, i.e. $J^-(z)\cap K=\emptyset$. The claim is that $u(z)=0$. If $J^-(z)\cap \operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u=\emptyset$, then $u(z)=0$ so there is nothing to prove. Assume therefore that the intersection is nonempty. Choose a time function $t$ as in \cref{prop:properties of ghstb}, with $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} f, \operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} v\subset t^{-1}([a,\infty))$ for some $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and assume without loss of generality that $t(z)\ge a$, otherwise the claim is trivial.

	Since $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u\cap J^-(z)$ is compact, we may choose $a'<\min_{q\in\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u\cap J^-(z)}t(q)$. Thus, the source and boundary datum vanish in $J^-(z)$ and $u$ vanishes with all its derivatives near $t=a'$ (inside $J^-(z)$). Then, for every $\tau\in[a',t(z)]$ consider the compact set
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lipschitz domain for energy estimate}
		\Omega_\tau\equiv J^-(z)\cap t^{-1}[a',\tau],
	\end{equation}
	and notice as well that, by \cref{lemma:slab-cone is a Lipschitz domain}, $\Omega_\tau$ is a Lipschitz region. Its boundary is given by the union of the four pieces
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:boundary of Lipschitz domain}
		\begin{aligned}
			T&=J^-(z)\cap \overline{\Sigma}_\tau,\quad B=J^-(z)\cap \overline{\Sigma}_{a'},\\
			W&=\Omega_\tau\cap \partial M,\quad C=(\partial J^-(z)\cap t^{-1}[a',\tau])\setminus W.
		\end{aligned}
	\end{equation}
	Depending on the relative position of the objects involved, it can happen that $W$ is a set of zero measure in $\partial \Omega_\tau$. In this case, the boundary condition is inessential and the result holds by the theory on boundaryless spacetimes. Otherwise, since $f$ and $v$ vanish on $J^-(z)$, we know that $u$ satisfies $Pu=0$ on $\Omega_\tau$ and $\gamma_0 u=0$ on $W$. Moreover, since $f, v$ and $u$ vanish on $t^{-1}(-\infty,a)$, we find an open neighbourhood $U$ of $\overline{\Sigma}_{a'}$ on which also $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u$ vanishes.

	Now we integrate \eqref{eq:current of SE tensor} over $\Omega_\tau$ and apply the divergence theorem (see \cite{mclean_strongly_2000}, Theorem 3.34, for a version for Lipschitz domains). Since $Pu=0$ in $\Omega_\tau$ we have (with $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} S$ denoting the surface measure)
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:divergence theorem for SE current}
		\begin{aligned}
			\int_{\Omega_\tau} R(u,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathrm{vol}_g&=\int_{\Omega_\tau}\operatorname{\mathrm{div}} \mathcal J[u]\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathrm{vol}_g=\int_{\partial\Omega_\tau}\braket{\nu,\mathcal J[u]}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} S\\
			&=\int_{T}\braket{\nu,\mathcal J[u]}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} S+\int_B\braket{\nu,\mathcal J[u]}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} S+\int_C\braket{\nu,\mathcal J[u]}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} S+\int_W\braket{\nu,\mathcal J[u]}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} S.
		\end{aligned}
	\end{equation}
	Since $u$ and $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u$ vanish in a neighbourhood of $\overline{\Sigma}_{a'}$, the contribution from $B$ is zero. Similarly, by \cref{lemma:stress-energy tensor for conormal direction}, the integral over $W$ is also zero. The very same result guarantees that the integral over $C$ is nonnegative, so we can neglect it to obtain, for the energy $E(\tau)=\int_T \mathcal J[u]\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} S$, the inequality
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:energy inequality 1}
		0\leq E(\tau)\leq \int_{\Omega_\tau} R(u,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathrm{vol}_g\leq c\int_{\Omega_\tau}|u|^2+|\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u|^2\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathrm{vol}_g,
	\end{equation}
	where we also used the continuity of $R$ to find the constant $c$.

	Now, since the exterior conormal to $T$ is simply $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t$, we have $E(\tau)=\int_T T_{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u}(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t,L^\flat)$ with $T_{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u}(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t,L^\flat)$ positive-definite. Then we find a uniform constant $c'$ such that $|T_{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u}(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t,L^\flat)|\ge c'|\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u|^2$. Consider then
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:energy at time tau}
		e(\tau)=\int_{\overline{\Sigma}_\tau\cap J^-(z)}|u|^2+|\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u|^2\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} S,
	\end{equation}
	which is an integrable function in view of Fubini. For a constant $c''$ we then have
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:estimate for du in the energy}
		\int_{\overline{\Sigma}_\tau\cap J^-(z)}|\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u|^2\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} S\leq c''\int_{a'}^\tau e(s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} s.
	\end{equation}
	A similar argument controls $\int_{\Omega_\tau}|u|^2\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathrm{vol}_g$: since $u$ vanishes on $\overline{\Sigma}_{a'}$, the fundamental theorem of calculus applied along the interval $[a',\tau]$ along an integral curve of $\nabla t$ gives, for every $x\in \overline{\Sigma}_\tau\cap J^-(z)$,
	\begin{equation}
		u(\tau,x)=\int_{a'}^\tau\partial_s u(s,x)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} s,
	\end{equation}
	whence by Cauchy--Schwarz we deduce that, for a constant $c^{(3)}$ independent of $x\in\overline{\Sigma}_\tau\cap J^-(z)$,
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:pointwise estimate of u on Sigma_tau}
		|u(\tau,x)|^2\le c^{(3)}\int_{a'}^\tau|\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u_{(s,x)}|^2\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} s.
	\end{equation}
	Integrating this estimate with respect to the Riemannian volume over $\overline{\Sigma}_\tau\cap J^-(z)$ leads to
	\begin{equation}
		\int_{\overline{\Sigma}_\tau\cap J^-(z)}|u|^2\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} S_{\tau}\le c^{(4)}\int_{a'}^\tau \int_{\Sigma_s\cap J^-(z)}|\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} u_{(s,x)}|^2\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} x\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} s,
	\end{equation}
	which is again controlled by the integral of $e$. Thus, with a new constant $\widetilde{c}$, we have
	\begin{equation}
		e(\tau)\le \widetilde{c}\int_{a'}^\tau e(s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} s,
	\end{equation}
	with $e(a')=0$. By Gronwall's lemma (applicable since $e$ is integrable and nonnegative) we deduce $e=0$, which in turn means that $u=0$ on $\overline{\Sigma}_\tau\cap J^-(z)$. Since $\tau$ was arbitrary in $[a',t(z)]$, this implies $u(z)=0$ and completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Since the spatially compact case is covered by \cref{cor:smooth existence}, assume that $\overline{M}$ is spatially noncompact.

	\textit{Step 1:} We begin by showing that to every $f\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$ and every $v\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\partial{M})$ there is a retarded solution $u$ of $Pu=f$ on $M$ and $\gamma_0 u=v$. Denote $C\equiv \operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} f\cup\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} v$, choose a splitting $\overline{M}=\mathbb{R}_t\times\overline{\Sigma}$ with noncompact Cauchy surface $\overline{\Sigma}$ and with a time function $t$ such that $C\subset\{t>a\}$ for some $a$. For any $T>a$ consider the subset (compact by global hyperbolicity)
	\begin{equation*}
		K_T\equiv J^+(C)\cap t^{-1}[a,T+1]
	\end{equation*}
	and denote by $S_T$ the projection of $K_T$ onto $\overline{\Sigma}$, also compact. Now we choose a compact smooth submanifold with boundary $\overline{U}_T$ of $\overline{\Sigma}$ such that
	\begin{enumerate}[i)]
		\item $S_T\subset\overline{U}_T$;
		\item $\partial \overline{U}_T$ is smooth and there is a neighbourhood of $S_T\cap\partial \Sigma$ in $\partial \Sigma$ on which $\partial U_T$ coincides with $\partial \Sigma$;
		\item the remaining portion of $\partial \overline{U}_T$ has positive distance from $S_T$.
	\end{enumerate}
	That is, $\partial\overline{U}_T$ is the union of a ``genuine'' part $\partial U^{gen}_T\subset \partial \Sigma$ and of an ``artificial'' part $\partial U^{art}_T\subset \Sigma$. Such a submanifold can be constructed by first taking an $\epsilon$-neighbourhood of $S_T$ in $\overline{\Sigma}$ and then smoothing out the corners that this creates away from $S_T\cap\partial\Sigma$.

	Let now $\overline{M}_T\equiv \mathbb{R}\times \overline{U}_T$ equipped with the restriction of the metric $g$. This is a spatially compact spacetime with timelike boundary (the normal to the boundary is clearly spacelike), with the same Cauchy time function $t$. For $v_T\equiv v$ on $\partial \overline{U}^{gen}_T$ and zero elsewhere on $\partial\overline{U}_T$, consider then the auxiliary problem
	\begin{equation}
		\left\{\begin{aligned}
			Pu&=f \quad \text{on }M,\\
			\gamma_0 u&=v_T.
		\end{aligned}\right.
	\end{equation}
	Being set up on a spatially compact globally hyperbolic spacetime with timelike boundary, this problem has a unique retarded solution $u_T\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M}_T)$, with support controlled by
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:support control in auxiliary spacetime}
	\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u_T\subset J^+_{\overline{M}_T}(C)\subset J^+_{\overline{M}}(C).
	\end{equation}
	Indeed, every causal curve in $\overline{M}_T$ is also causal in $\overline{M}$. Moreover, by construction, $\partial\overline{U}_T^{art}$ is disjoint from $J^+_{\overline{M}}(C)\cap t^{-1}(-\infty,T+1]$, so that \eqref{eq:support control in auxiliary spacetime} gives that $u_T$ vanishes in a neighbourhood of $(-\infty,T]\times \partial U^{art}_T$, so it can be extended by zero across it. This shows that $u_T$ is a solution of the original problem on $(-\infty,T]\times \overline{\Sigma}$.

	If we were to choose a different neighbourhood $\overline{U}_T'$ or a different $T'>T$, the constructed solution would not change on the smaller domains. Indeed, for example (the case of a different $T'$ is completely analogous), if $\overline{U}'_T$ is a (say larger) submanifold of $\overline{\Sigma}$ satisfying the same properties as $\overline{U}_T$, and $u_T'$ is the solution constructed by the above procedure on it, then the difference $w=u_T-u_T'$ satisfies $Pw=0$ and $\gamma_0 w=0$ on the smaller domain $\overline{U}_T$. By \cref{theo:support of solutions}, $w=0$ on $\overline{U}_T$ which shows that the solution is independent of the choice of $\overline{U}_T$. Then, choose a monotone sequence $(T_j)\to\infty$ and define
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:solution to noncompact problem}
		u(q)\equiv u_{T_j}(q) \quad \text{for any }j\text{ with }T_j>t(q).
	\end{equation}
	By construction, $u$ is a well-defined smooth function, solving $Pu=f$ and $\gamma_0 u=v$ on $\overline{M}$. By the support estimate of \cref{theo:support of solutions} we have $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u\subset J^+(C)$, so that $u$ is past-compact (in fact strictly so in this case).

	\textit{Step 2:} We now let $f\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$ and $v\in\mathit C^{\infty}_\mathrm{pc}(\partial M)$ be general. Denote again by $C$ the union of the supports of $f$ and $v$. If $K$ is any compact set in $\overline{M}$, consider the compact set $C_K\equiv C\cap J^-(K)$ and choose a cutoff $\chi_K\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$, equal to one in a neighbourhood of $C_K$. Then the problem with compactly supported data
	\begin{equation}
		\left\{\begin{aligned}
			Pu&=\chi_K f,\\
			\gamma_0 u&=(\gamma_0 \chi_K)v,
		\end{aligned}\right.
	\end{equation}
	has, by Step 1, a unique retarded solution $u_K$, whose restriction to $K$ is independent of the choice of $\chi_K$. Indeed, if $\chi_K'$ were another cutoff with the same properties, the difference of data would vanish on $J^-(K)$, so that by uniqueness/finite propagation speed the solutions would coincide on $K$.

	Take now a compact exhaustion $\bigcup_{j}K_j=\overline{M}$ and define
	\begin{equation}
		u(q)\equiv u_{K_j}(q),\quad \text{if }q\in K_j.
	\end{equation}
	The function $u$ is well-defined by the argument above, solves the required problem on $\overline{M}$, and has past-compact support by construction. This finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
We begin by showing that to every $f\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$ and every $v\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\partial{M})$ there is a retarded solution $u$ of $Pu=f$ on $M$ and $\gamma_0 u=v$. Denote $C\equiv \operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} f\cup\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} v$, choose a splitting $\overline{M}=\mathbb{R}_t\times\overline{\Sigma}$ with noncompact Cauchy surface $\overline{\Sigma}$ and with a time function $t$ such that $C\subset\{t>a\}$ for some $a$. For any $T>a$ consider the subset (compact by global hyperbolicity)
	\begin{equation*}
		K_T\equiv J^+(C)\cap t^{-1}[a,T+1]
	\end{equation*}
	and denote by $S_T$ the projection of $K_T$ onto $\overline{\Sigma}$, also compact. Now we choose a compact smooth submanifold with boundary $\overline{U}_T$ of $\overline{\Sigma}$ such that
	\begin{enumerate}[i)]
		\item $S_T\subset\overline{U}_T$;
		\item $\partial \overline{U}_T$ is smooth and there is a neighbourhood of $S_T\cap\partial \Sigma$ in $\partial \Sigma$ on which $\partial U_T$ coincides with $\partial \Sigma$;
		\item the remaining portion of $\partial \overline{U}_T$ has positive distance from $S_T$.
	\end{enumerate}
	That is, $\partial\overline{U}_T$ is the union of a ``genuine'' part $\partial U^{gen}_T\subset \partial \Sigma$ and of an ``artificial'' part $\partial U^{art}_T\subset \Sigma$. Such a submanifold can be constructed by first taking an $\epsilon$-neighbourhood of $S_T$ in $\overline{\Sigma}$ and then smoothing out the corners that this creates away from $S_T\cap\partial\Sigma$.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
We now let $f\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$ and $v\in\mathit C^{\infty}_\mathrm{pc}(\partial M)$ be general. Denote again by $C$ the union of the supports of $f$ and $v$. If $K$ is any compact set in $\overline{M}$, consider the compact set $C_K\equiv C\cap J^-(K)$ and choose a cutoff $\chi_K\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$, equal to one in a neighbourhood of $C_K$. Then the problem with compactly supported data
	\begin{equation}
		\left\{\begin{aligned}
			Pu&=\chi_K f,\\
			\gamma_0 u&=(\gamma_0 \chi_K)v,
		\end{aligned}\right.
	\end{equation}
	has, by Step 1, a unique retarded solution $u_K$, whose restriction to $K$ is independent of the choice of $\chi_K$. Indeed, if $\chi_K'$ were another cutoff with the same properties, the difference of data would vanish on $J^-(K)$, so that by uniqueness/finite propagation speed the solutions would coincide on $K$.
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
The proof of \cref{theo:propagators} above works as well for compactly supported distributional sources $f\in\dot\mathscr{E}'(\overline{M})$ and produces distributional solutions $u\in\dot{\mathscr{D}}'_{\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$. Indeed, local existence and uniqueness are obtained by duality from \cref{theo:existence and uniqueness}, using that $P$ is formally self-adjoint. For the global statement, notice that a distribution can be restricted to open subsets of $\overline{M}$ and that this is all that is required to apply the exhaustion argument.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:fundamental solution for retarded BVP}
	There exist bounded operators $\widetilde{G}^\pm_D\colon \mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}/\mathrm{fc}}(\overline{M})\oplus\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}/\mathrm{fc}}(\partial M)\to\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}/\mathrm{fc}}(\overline{M})$ that are inverses to $(P,\gamma_0)$. More precisely,
	\begin{align*}
		(P,\gamma_0)\widetilde{G}^+_D(f,v)&=(f,v),\qquad \widetilde{G}^+_D(P,\gamma_0)u=u,\qquad u,f,v\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}},\\
		(P,\gamma_0)\widetilde{G}^-_D(f,v)&=(f,v),\qquad\widetilde{G}^-_D(P,\gamma_0)u=u,\qquad u,f,v\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{fc}}.
	\end{align*}
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lemma:exact sequence}
	The following sequence is exact:
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:exact sequence}
		0\to \mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})\xrightarrow{(P,\gamma_0)}
		\begin{array}{c}
			\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M}) \\
			\oplus \\
			\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\partial M)
		\end{array}
		\xrightarrow{\widetilde{G}_D}\mathit C^{\infty}_{D,\mathrm{sc}}(\overline{M})\xrightarrow{P}\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{sc}}(\overline{M}).
	\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The proof is a quick adaptation of the proof for the boundaryless case by employing the propagator $\widetilde{G}_D$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item Exactness at $\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$ amounts to injectivity of $(P,\gamma_0)$ on this domain. However, $(P,\gamma_0)$ is invertible on the larger domain $\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$ with inverse $\widetilde{G}^+_D$, therefore its restriction to $\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$ is certainly injective.

		\item Exactness at $\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})\oplus\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\partial M)$ corresponds to having $\operatorname{\mathrm{ran}}((P,\gamma_0)|_{\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})})=\ker \widetilde{G}_D$.
		To see this, first let $u\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$ and consider $(f,v)=(Pu,\gamma_0u)\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})\oplus\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\partial M)$. Then $\widetilde{G}_D(f,v)=\widetilde{G}_D^+(f,v)-\widetilde{G}^-_D(f,v)=u-u=0$, having used that $\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})\subset\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}\cap\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{fc}}$.
