		On the other hand, assume that for some $(f,v)\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})\oplus\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\partial M)$ we have $\widetilde{G}_D(f,v)=0$, that is $\widetilde{G}_D^+(f,v)=\widetilde{G}_D^-(f,v)$. The right-hand side being strictly future-compact and the left-hand side strictly past-compact, we have that $u\equiv \widetilde{G}^+_D(f,v)$ is compactly supported, and by definition it satisfies $Pu=f,\gamma_0u=v$. This proves the claim.

		\item We need to show $\operatorname{\mathrm{ran}}(\widetilde{G}_D)=\ker P|_{\mathit C^{\infty}_{D,\mathrm{sc}}}$. First, if $u=\widetilde{G}_D(f,v)$, we already remarked that $(P,\gamma_0)\widetilde{G}_D^\pm(f,v)=(f,v)$, so that the difference of the two vanishes. For the opposite inclusion, let $u\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{D,\mathrm{sc}}(\overline{M})$ satisfy $Pu=0$. We fix a past cutoff function $\chi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$, with $1-\chi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{fc}}(\overline{M})$, and consider $Pu=P(\chi u)+P((1-\chi)u)=f^++f^-$, where $f^+\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}$, $f^-\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{fc}}$. Since $Pu=0$, we have $f^+=-f^-$, moreover $\chi u=\widetilde{G}^+_D f^+$ and $(1-\chi)u=\widetilde{G}^-_Df^-$. Then, $f\equiv f^+$ satisfies
		\begin{align*}
			\widetilde{G}_Df&=\widetilde{G}^+_Df^+-\widetilde{G}^-_Df^+=\widetilde{G}^+_Df^++\widetilde{G}^-_Df^-\\
			&=\chi u+(1-\chi)u=u,
		\end{align*}
		proving the claim.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
\label{rem:supports and exact sequence}
	In \eqref{eq:exact sequence} it is important to consider functions whose compact supports \textit{can} intersect the boundary. Indeed, the formulation above must be invariant under the time evolution, so that the function spaces themselves have to be. However, as remarked in the Introduction, $\mathit C^{\infty}_c(M)$ is not invariant, as under time evolution the supports propagate and eventually reach the boundary. Notice as well that exactness at $\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$ corresponds to the classical fact that the only solution to the wave equation with vanishing source and compact support is the zero function. Here, of course, the boundary condition plays the role of restoring this injectivity.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lemma:G_D is a symplectic form}
	For $[u],[v]\in \mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})/P\mathit C^{\infty}_{D,c}(\overline{M})$ define the bilinear form
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:symplectic form on solutions}
		\omega([u],[v])=\int_{\overline{M}}u G_Dv \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathrm{vol}_g.
	\end{equation}
	Then $\omega$ is symplectic, i.e. skew-symmetric and nondegenerate. It induces therefore a symplectic form on $\ker_D P$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Since the operator $P$ is formally self-adjoint and solutions satisfy the homogeneous Dirichlet boundary condition, the inverses of $P$ satisfy $(G^\pm_D)^t= G^\mp_D$ on $\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$. Hence, on its domain, $G_D$ is skew-symmetric, $G_D^t=-G_D$. On the other hand, let $[u]\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{c}(\overline{M})/P\mathit C^{\infty}_{D,c}(\overline{M})$ satisfy $\omega([u],[v])=(u,G_D v)=0$ for all $v\in \mathit C^{\infty}_{c}(\overline{M})$. Then, after transposing, we must have $G_Du=0$ by nondegeneracy of the inner product of $L^2(M)$. By \cref{lemma:exact sequence} we find $w\in \mathit C^{\infty}_{D,c}(\overline{M})$ with $u=Pw$, so $[u]=0$. This finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
\label{def:causal compressed b-covectors}
	Fix $q\in\partial M$. A covector $\alpha\in{\widetilde{T}_q^\ast}\overline{M}$ is called causal if it is the image of a causal covector $\beta\in T_q^\ast \overline{M}$ under $\varrho^t$. A covector $\alpha\in\widetilde{T}^\ast_q\overline{M}$ is called spacelike if it is not causal. Equivalently, $\alpha$ is spacelike if all its preimages via $\varrho^t$ are spacelike covectors in $T^\ast_q\overline{M}$.

	For $\alpha$ a causal covector in ${\widetilde{T}_q^\ast}\overline{M}$, we say that it is \textit{future-directed} (resp.\ past-directed) if it is the image of a future-directed (resp.\ past-directed) causal covector in $\mathit{T}^{\ast\!}_q\overline{M}$ under $\varrho^t$. Equivalently, for some Cauchy temporal function $t$ chosen near $q$ and some causal covector $\beta\in T^\ast_q\overline{M}$ with $\varrho^t(\beta)=\alpha$, we have $g^{-1}_q(\beta,\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t)>0$. The set of compressed causal covectors over all points of $\overline{M}$, $\widetilde{V}\overline{M}$, is a cone bundle, which splits, after removing the zero section, into two disjoint connected components $\widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$ and $\widetilde{V}^-\overline{M}$, comprising respectively all future-directed and past-directed compressed causal covectors over points of $\overline{M}$.

	The above definitions are invariant along rays in the cotangent directions in ${}^{\mathit{b}}\!\mathit{T}^{\ast\!} \overline{M}$, thus the sets of future- and past-directed causal covectors are conic. The same terminology will therefore be used to speak about oriented directions in the \textit{compressed cosphere bundle} ${\widetilde{\operatorname{\mathbb S}}^\ast}\!{\overline{M}}$, i.e. the quotient by the scaling action.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
\label{rem:compressed causal cone}
	The reason why we do not distinguish between time- and lightlike covectors in ${\widetilde{T}^\ast}\overline{M}$ is that, under the anchor map, both some lightlike and some timelike covectors have the same image in ${}^{\mathit{b}}\!\mathit{T}^{\ast\!}\overline{M}$. This will however not cause any difficulty, since we are only interested in the fact that the singularities of a solution $u$ are constrained to keep their time-orientation. In fact, over a boundary point $q$, the image via $\varrho^t$ of the light cone $\{(\tau,\xi,\eta)\in T^ \ast_q\overline{M}\colon \tau^2=\xi^2+|\eta|^2\}$ is exactly the compressed causal cone $\widetilde{V}_q\overline{M}=\{(\tau,0,\eta)\in\widetilde{T}_q^\ast \overline{M}\colon \tau^2\geq |\eta|^2\}$.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- lemma-18: body_md -->
\label{lemma:distributional uniqueness for the retarded BVP}
	Let $u\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ be past-compact and satisfy $Pu=0$, $\gamma_0u=0$.
	Then $u=0$.
<!-- end lemma-18 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
By \cref{theo:smoothness and solvability in N'} (1), $u$ has well-defined traces
	$\gamma_ju=(\partial_x^ju)|_{x=0}\in\mathscr{D}'(\partial M)$, and by
	\cref{lemma:extensible=supported for dual-conormal} it has a unique supported
	representative, so $\braket{u,\varphi}$ is defined for all $\varphi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$.

	Let $\chi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$ and set $w=G^-_D\chi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{sfc}}(\overline{M})$, so that
	$Pw=\chi$, $\gamma_0w=0$, $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} w\subset J^-(\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}\chi)$. As $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u$ is
	past-compact and $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} w$ strictly future-compact, $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u\cap\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} w$ is
	compact; pick $\theta\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$ with $\theta\equiv1$ near it and put
	$W=\theta w\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$, which still satisfies $\gamma_0W=0$. Since
	$PW=\theta\chi+[P,\theta]w$ and $\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}([P,\theta]w)\cap\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}} u=\emptyset$, we get
	$\braket{u,\chi}=\braket{u,PW}$. Green's identity for the formally self-adjoint $P$,
	\[
	\braket{u,PW}-\braket{Pu,W}
	=\braket{\gamma_1u,\gamma_0W}_{\partial M}-\braket{\gamma_0u,\gamma_1W}_{\partial M},
	\]
	holds for $u\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ and $W\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$: integrate by parts on
	$\{x\ge\delta\}$ and let $\delta\downarrow0$, the boundary terms converging because
	$u$ is a smooth function of $x$ with values in $\mathscr{D}'(\partial M)$. Both right-hand
	terms vanish and $Pu=0$, so $\braket{u,\chi}=0$ for all $\chi$, i.e. $u=0$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{theo:singularities of the BVP}
	Let $P$ be scalar and normally hyperbolic, and assume we have $u\in \mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ solving $Pu=0, \gamma_0 u=0$. Then $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)\subset\widetilde{V}\overline{M}$.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
In the interior, this is part of the standard theory. At the boundary, it suffices to argue locally. Moreover, the conditions only depend on the principal symbols. Therefore we are, after localisation, exactly in the situation of \cref{theo:DBC satisfies LS}. The proof is finished since the set $\operatorname{\mathrm{Char}}(P;B)$ computed there is, in local adapted coordinates, precisely the compressed causal cone bundle, see \cref{rem:compressed causal cone}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{theo:propagation of future singularities}
	Let $\overline{M}$ be a globally hyperbolic spacetime with timelike boundary, $\overline{\Sigma}$ any Cauchy surface in $\overline{M}$. Assume that $u\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ is a solution to
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:vanishing mixed problem}
		\left\{\begin{aligned}
			P u&=0\\
			u|_{\partial M}&=0.
		\end{aligned}\right.
	\end{equation}
	Assume furthermore that there is an open neighbourhood $\mathcal U\simeq (-1,1)\times \overline{\Sigma}$ of $\overline{\Sigma}$ such that $\mathsf{WF}_b(u|_{\mathcal U})\subset \widetilde{V}^+{\mathcal U}$. Then, $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)\subset \widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$. Moreover, the same is true in the Hilbert-space-valued case.
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
We divide the proof in several steps.
	
	\emph{Step 1: Microlocal splitting.} We decompose $u$ according to the time-orientation of its singularities. To this end, we cover $\widetilde{\mathbb{S}^{\ast\!}}{\overline{M}}\subset{}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}\overline{M}$ with open sets $U_+,U_-,U_s$, as follows:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $U_+$ is a small open neighbourhood (in ${}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}\overline{M}$) of the set $K_+=\{[\varsigma]\in{\widetilde{\operatorname{\mathbb S}}^\ast}\!{\overline{M}}\colon \varsigma\in \widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}\}$ with $U_+\cap K_-=\emptyset$;
		\item $U_-$ is an open neighbourhood of $K_-$, which is the same as $K_+$ but with $\varsigma\in \widetilde{V}^-\overline{M}$, and $U_-$ does not intersect $U_+$;
		\item $U_s$ is any open set in ${}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}\overline{M}$, not intersecting $K_+\cup K_-$ and such that $\{U_+,U_-,U_s\}$ covers ${}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}\overline{M}$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Sets as above can be constructed by choosing a Riemannian metric on ${}^{\mathit b}T^{\ast}\overline{M}$ and taking $\epsilon$-neighbourhoods of $K_\pm$. Notice as well that $K_+$ and $K_-$ are closed and disjoint subsets of ${}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}\overline{M}$. Figure \cref{fig:microlocal partition} depicts, for $q\in\partial M$, the compressed causal cone in ${}^{\mathit b}T^{\ast}_q\overline{M}$ and the neighbourhoods $U_\bullet$ that we use.

					\clip (0,0) circle[radius=1.5cm];

						\draw[cfutf,opacity=.45,line width=12pt,line cap=round]
						plot[variable=\th,domain=-45:45,samples=55,smooth] (0,{sin(\th)},{cos(\th)});
						\draw[cpastf,opacity=.45,line width=12pt,line cap=round]
						plot[variable=\th,domain=135:225,samples=55,smooth] (0,{sin(\th)},{cos(\th)});
					\end{scope}

				\begin{scope}[bproj]
					\draw[eq]
					plot[variable=\th,domain=-30:150,samples=95,smooth] (0,{sin(\th)},{cos(\th)});

					plot[variable=\th,domain=-30:45,samples=45,smooth] (0,{sin(\th)},{cos(\th)});
					\draw[cpast,line width=1.4pt]
					plot[variable=\th,domain=135:150,samples=20,smooth] (0,{sin(\th)},{cos(\th)});

				\node[slbl,text=cfut,anchor=north]  at (0, 1.16) {$K_+\cap {}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}_q\overline{M}$};
				\node[slbl,text=cpast,anchor=south] at (0,-1.16) {$K_-\cap {}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}_q\overline{M}$};

				\node[lbl,text=cs,anchor=west] at ( 2.14, 0.85) {$U_s\cap {}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}_q\overline{M}$};

	Pick a $b$-microlocal partition of unity subordinate to this cover, $\{B_+,B_-,B_s\}$, and write $I=B_++B_-+B_s$ up to an operator in $\Psi_b^{-\infty}(\overline{M})$. Since each $B_\bullet$ preserves $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$, we obtain distributions $u_\bullet=B_\bullet u\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ for $\bullet\in\{+,-,s\}$, microlocalised in the corresponding set and satisfying $u=u_++u_-+u_s\mod\mathscr{A}(\overline{M})$.

	\emph{Step 2: Smoothness of the spacelike part.} We now claim that $u_s$ is smooth: on the one hand, by definition of $B_s$, the $b$-wave-front set of $u_s$ does not intersect $\widetilde{V}^\pm\overline{M}$, on the other we have $\mathsf{WF}_b(u_s)\subset\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$ by \cref{lemma:properties of b-wave-front set}, so that $\mathsf{WF}_b(u_s)\subset \widetilde{V}\overline{M}$. Therefore $\mathsf{WF}_b(u_s)$ is empty, so that $u_s\in\mathscr{A}(\overline{M})$.

	\emph{Step 3: Uniqueness of the splitting.} The splitting $u=u_++u_-$ is then unique up to $\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M})$. Indeed, if $\widetilde{u}_++\widetilde{u}_-$ is another such splitting, then
	\[
	u_+-\widetilde{u}_+=\widetilde{u}_--u_-\mod \mathscr{A}(\overline{M}).
	\]
	Since the distributions $u_+-\widetilde{u}_+$ and $u_--\widetilde{u}_-$ are microlocalised, respectively, in $\widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$ and $\widetilde{V}^-\overline{M}$, and $\widetilde{V}^-\overline{M}\cap \widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$ is empty, the $b$-wave-front sets of the two sides both have to be empty. Thus,
	\[
	\widetilde{u}_+-u_+\in{\mathscr{A}}(\overline{M})\cap\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})=\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M}),
	\]
	proving essential uniqueness of the splitting.

	\emph{Step 4: Regularity of $Pu_\pm$.} The equation $Pu=0$ implies that $Pu_+=-P u_-\mod\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M})$ and $\mathsf{WF}_b(Pu_\bullet)\subset \mathsf{WF}_b(u_\bullet)$ by \cref{lemma:properties of b-wave-front set}, so that the $b$-wave-front set of either side has to be empty. Thus, by construction, $P u_{\pm}\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M})$.

	\emph{Step 5: Smoothness of $u_-$ in the future.} Choose now a time function $t\colon \overline{M}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ for which $\mathcal{U}\supset t^{-1}(-1,1)$ ($\mathcal U$ being the neighbourhood in the assumption) and a cutoff $\psi\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M},[0,1])$ such that
	\[\begin{aligned}
		\psi(q)&\equiv 0 \quad\text{if}\quad t(q)<-1, \\
		\psi(q)&\equiv 1 \quad\text{if}\quad t(q)>1.
	\end{aligned}\]
	Then $v_-\equiv\psi u_-\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ satisfies $v_-\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\mathcal{U})$ and $v_-\equiv0$ on $t^{-1}(-\infty,-1)$. Moreover, $P v_-=f_-\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$. Indeed,
	\begin{equation*}
		Pv_-=\psi P u_-+[P,\psi]u_-,
	\end{equation*}
	where the first term is smooth by the previous paragraph, while $[P,\psi]$ has nonzero coefficients only in $\{-1\le t\le1\}\subset\mathcal U$, where $u_-$ is smooth.

	An analogous argument shows that $\gamma_0u_\pm\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\partial M)$. Recall first that since $u_\bullet\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$, the
	restrictions $\gamma_0u_\bullet\in\mathscr{D}'(\partial M)$ are well defined by
	\cref{prop:restriction and boundary WF set}. Applying $\gamma_0$ to
	$u=u_++u_-\mod\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M})$ and using $\gamma_0u=0$ gives
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:traces of the two halves}
		\gamma_0u_+=-\gamma_0u_-\mod\mathit C^{\infty}(\partial M).
	\end{equation}
	On the other hand $\mathsf{WF}_b(u_\pm)\subset\widetilde{V}^\pm\overline{M}$ by definition of the microlocal partition of unity, so that
	\cref{prop:restriction and boundary WF set} yields
	\[
	\mathsf{WF}(\gamma_0u_\pm)\subset\partial\mathsf{WF}(u_\pm)
	\subset\widetilde{V}^\pm\overline{M}.
	\]
	Since the sets $\widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$ and $\widetilde{V}^-\overline{M}$ are disjoint we must have $\mathsf{WF}(\gamma_0u_+)=\mathsf{WF}(\gamma_0u_-)$, so both are empty and
	$\gamma_0u_\pm\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\partial M)$.

	Consequently $\gamma_0v_-=(\psi|_{\partial M})\,\gamma_0u_-$ is smooth and vanishes for $t<-1$, that is, $\gamma_0v_-\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\partial M)$. Let $w\equiv\widetilde{G}^+_D(f_-,\gamma_0v_-)\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$ be the smooth solution given by \cref{cor:fundamental solution for retarded BVP}. Then $w-v_-$ is past-compact, lies in $\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ and satisfies $P(w-v_-)=0$, $\gamma_0(w-v_-)=0$, so that by \cref{lemma:distributional uniqueness for the retarded BVP} it vanishes. That is, $v_-=w\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$, which means in particular that $u_-$ is smooth for $t>1$, since $\psi=1$ there.

	\emph{Step 6: End of the proof.} The analogous argument for the advanced problem applies to $(1-\psi)u_-$ and shows that $u_-\in\mathit C^{\infty}(t^{-1}(-\infty,-1))$, and thus everywhere, away from $t^{-1}(\{-1,1\})$. However, we may always choose another cutoff $\widetilde{\psi}$ with $\widetilde{\psi}=0$ on $t^{-1}(-\infty,-1+\varepsilon)$ and $\widetilde{\psi}=1$ on $t^{-1}(1-\varepsilon,\infty)$, and the same argument shows that $u_-$ is smooth away from $\{t=-1+\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon\}$. Thus, $u_-$ is in fact smooth everywhere. As a consequence, we have $u=u_+\mod\mathscr{A}(\overline{M})$ and $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)=\mathsf{WF}_b(u_+)\subset\widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$, which is the claim for the scalar case. If $u$ takes values in a Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, the same computation shows that, for any $v\in\mathcal H$, $\mathsf{WF}_b((v,u))\subset \widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$. By \cref{theo:weak and strong b-wave-front set}, $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)=\overline{\cup_{v\in\mathcal H}\mathsf{WF}_b((v,u))}$, and since $\widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$ is closed we find that $u$ only has future-directed singularities. This concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
We decompose $u$ according to the time-orientation of its singularities. To this end, we cover $\widetilde{\mathbb{S}^{\ast\!}}{\overline{M}}\subset{}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}\overline{M}$ with open sets $U_+,U_-,U_s$, as follows:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $U_+$ is a small open neighbourhood (in ${}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}\overline{M}$) of the set $K_+=\{[\varsigma]\in{\widetilde{\operatorname{\mathbb S}}^\ast}\!{\overline{M}}\colon \varsigma\in \widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}\}$ with $U_+\cap K_-=\emptyset$;
		\item $U_-$ is an open neighbourhood of $K_-$, which is the same as $K_+$ but with $\varsigma\in \widetilde{V}^-\overline{M}$, and $U_-$ does not intersect $U_+$;
		\item $U_s$ is any open set in ${}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}\overline{M}$, not intersecting $K_+\cup K_-$ and such that $\{U_+,U_-,U_s\}$ covers ${}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}\overline{M}$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Sets as above can be constructed by choosing a Riemannian metric on ${}^{\mathit b}T^{\ast}\overline{M}$ and taking $\epsilon$-neighbourhoods of $K_\pm$. Notice as well that $K_+$ and $K_-$ are closed and disjoint subsets of ${}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}\overline{M}$. Figure \cref{fig:microlocal partition} depicts, for $q\in\partial M$, the compressed causal cone in ${}^{\mathit b}T^{\ast}_q\overline{M}$ and the neighbourhoods $U_\bullet$ that we use.
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- head-4: body_md -->
We now claim that $u_s$ is smooth: on the one hand, by definition of $B_s$, the $b$-wave-front set of $u_s$ does not intersect $\widetilde{V}^\pm\overline{M}$, on the other we have $\mathsf{WF}_b(u_s)\subset\mathsf{WF}_b(u)$ by \cref{lemma:properties of b-wave-front set}, so that $\mathsf{WF}_b(u_s)\subset \widetilde{V}\overline{M}$. Therefore $\mathsf{WF}_b(u_s)$ is empty, so that $u_s\in\mathscr{A}(\overline{M})$.
<!-- end head-4 -->
<!-- head-5: body_md -->
The splitting $u=u_++u_-$ is then unique up to $\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M})$. Indeed, if $\widetilde{u}_++\widetilde{u}_-$ is another such splitting, then
	\[
	u_+-\widetilde{u}_+=\widetilde{u}_--u_-\mod \mathscr{A}(\overline{M}).
	\]
	Since the distributions $u_+-\widetilde{u}_+$ and $u_--\widetilde{u}_-$ are microlocalised, respectively, in $\widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$ and $\widetilde{V}^-\overline{M}$, and $\widetilde{V}^-\overline{M}\cap \widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$ is empty, the $b$-wave-front sets of the two sides both have to be empty. Thus,
	\[
	\widetilde{u}_+-u_+\in{\mathscr{A}}(\overline{M})\cap\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})=\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M}),
	\]
	proving essential uniqueness of the splitting.
<!-- end head-5 -->
<!-- head-6: body_md -->
The equation $Pu=0$ implies that $Pu_+=-P u_-\mod\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M})$ and $\mathsf{WF}_b(Pu_\bullet)\subset \mathsf{WF}_b(u_\bullet)$ by \cref{lemma:properties of b-wave-front set}, so that the $b$-wave-front set of either side has to be empty. Thus, by construction, $P u_{\pm}\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M})$.
<!-- end head-6 -->
<!-- head-7: body_md -->
Choose now a time function $t\colon \overline{M}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ for which $\mathcal{U}\supset t^{-1}(-1,1)$ ($\mathcal U$ being the neighbourhood in the assumption) and a cutoff $\psi\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M},[0,1])$ such that
	\[\begin{aligned}
		\psi(q)&\equiv 0 \quad\text{if}\quad t(q)<-1, \\
		\psi(q)&\equiv 1 \quad\text{if}\quad t(q)>1.
	\end{aligned}\]
	Then $v_-\equiv\psi u_-\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$ satisfies $v_-\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\mathcal{U})$ and $v_-\equiv0$ on $t^{-1}(-\infty,-1)$. Moreover, $P v_-=f_-\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{\mathrm{pc}}(\overline{M})$. Indeed,
	\begin{equation*}
		Pv_-=\psi P u_-+[P,\psi]u_-,
	\end{equation*}
	where the first term is smooth by the previous paragraph, while $[P,\psi]$ has nonzero coefficients only in $\{-1\le t\le1\}\subset\mathcal U$, where $u_-$ is smooth.
<!-- end head-7 -->
<!-- head-8: body_md -->
The analogous argument for the advanced problem applies to $(1-\psi)u_-$ and shows that $u_-\in\mathit C^{\infty}(t^{-1}(-\infty,-1))$, and thus everywhere, away from $t^{-1}(\{-1,1\})$. However, we may always choose another cutoff $\widetilde{\psi}$ with $\widetilde{\psi}=0$ on $t^{-1}(-\infty,-1+\varepsilon)$ and $\widetilde{\psi}=1$ on $t^{-1}(1-\varepsilon,\infty)$, and the same argument shows that $u_-$ is smooth away from $\{t=-1+\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon\}$. Thus, $u_-$ is in fact smooth everywhere. As a consequence, we have $u=u_+\mod\mathscr{A}(\overline{M})$ and $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)=\mathsf{WF}_b(u_+)\subset\widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$, which is the claim for the scalar case. If $u$ takes values in a Hilbert space $\mathcal H$, the same computation shows that, for any $v\in\mathcal H$, $\mathsf{WF}_b((v,u))\subset \widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$. By \cref{theo:weak and strong b-wave-front set}, $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)=\overline{\cup_{v\in\mathcal H}\mathsf{WF}_b((v,u))}$, and since $\widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$ is closed we find that $u$ only has future-directed singularities. This concludes the proof.
<!-- end head-8 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{theo:propagator is a solution}
	$\Phi$ is a distributional solution of
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:BVP for causal propagator}
		\left\{\begin{aligned}
			Pu&=0\quad\text{on }M\\
			\gamma_0 u&=0.
		\end{aligned}\right.
	\end{equation}
	That is, it is an element of $\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$, it satisfies $\Phi(P\varphi)=0$ for all $\varphi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{D,c}(\overline{M})$ and $\gamma_0\Phi(\psi)=0$ for all $\psi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\partial M)$, both equations holding between elements of $H_+$.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
That $\Phi(P\varphi)=0$ for all $\varphi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_{D,c}(\overline{M})$ is a direct consequence of the above discussion. Then, by \cref{cor:kernel of NHO is normally regular}, $\Phi\in \mathscr{N}(\overline{M};H_+)$, so that, for any choice of boundary defining function $x$, $\Phi$ is a smooth family of distributions on $\partial M$, parametrised by $x$. Thus, it restricts strongly to $x=0$ to give a distribution $u_0\in\mathscr{D}'(\partial M;H_+)$. More precisely, $\Phi$ has a Taylor expansion in $x$ with coefficients $u_k=\frac{1}{k!}\partial^k_x (p G_D)|_{x=0}\in\mathscr{D}'(\partial M;H_+)$:
	\begin{equation}
		\Phi=u_0+xu_1+\dots.
	\end{equation}
	The restriction to $\partial M$ is simply the $H_+$-valued distribution $u_0$. For $\psi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\partial M)$, the pairing $\braket{u_0,\psi}$ is then $pG_D(\psi\otimes \delta)$ (notice that this is well-defined since $\psi\otimes\delta_{\partial M}$ is conormal to $\partial M$ and $\mathscr{N}\subset\mathscr{A}'$), and the claim is that this vanishes. Notice that the operator $G_D$ has a distributional kernel $K_D\in\dot\mathscr{D}'(\overline{M}\times\overline{M})$, which satisfies the Dirichlet boundary condition in the first component, i.e. $\gamma_0^{(1)}K_D=0$ (the restriction being well-defined in view of normal regularity). Indeed, the range of $G_D$ consist precisely of functions solving the homogeneous Klein--Gordon equation with vanishing Dirichlet trace. Since $G_D$ is skew-adjoint as in \cref{lemma:G_D is a symplectic form}, $K_D$ satisfies the Dirichlet condition in the second component as well, i.e. $\gamma_0^{(2)}K_D=0$.

	For any $\psi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\partial M)$, we have thus
	\begin{equation*}
		\braket{pG_D(\psi\otimes\delta_{\partial M}),f}=\braket{K_D,f\otimes \gamma_0^\ast\psi}=(\gamma_0^{(2)}K_D)(f,\psi)=0.
	\end{equation*}
	Since $p$ is a linear and continuous map it follows that $\gamma_0\Phi$ itself must vanish. This proves the assertion.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
\label{def:hadamard states for Dirichlet}
	We say that a centred quasi-free state $\omega$ on
	$\mathfrak{U}(P,\overline{M})$ is a \textit{Dirichlet--Hadamard state}
	if $\Phi_\omega\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M};H_\omega)$ and we have
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:hadamard states}
		\mathsf{WF}_b(\Phi_\omega)\subset\widetilde{V}^+\overline{M} .
	\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rem:hadamard condition}
	In view of the aforementioned \cref{prop:properties of b-WF for HS-distributions}, the proposed Dirichlet--Hadamard condition is the natural analogue of the microlocal Hadamard condition of \textcite{radzikowski_micro-local_1996}, as reformulated in \cite{strohmaier_reeh-schlieder_2002}. Importantly, this reformulation allows us to do away with considerations of corners.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{theo:uniqueness of hadamard states}
	Let $\omega$ and $\omega'$ be quasi-free Dirichlet--Hadamard states on
	$\mathfrak{U}(\overline{M})$, with one-particle distributions $\Phi$, $\Phi'$ and
	two-point functions $\omega_2$, $\omega_2'$. Then
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:uniqueness of hadamard states}
		\omega_2-\omega_2'\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M}\times\overline{M}).
	\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
Recall, in the proof, the convention that we use coordinates $\zeta=(\lambda,\eta)$ with $\lambda=\xi+\mathrm{i} L$, and analyse the behaviour of the Mellin--Fourier transform for fixed $L$ and $|(\xi,\eta)|\to\infty$.
	
	Denote by $H_+$ and $H_+'$ the two one-particle Hilbert spaces and set
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:doubled one-particle distribution}
		\mathcal H=H_+\oplus H_+',\qquad
		\Psi=\Phi\oplus\Phi',\qquad
		K=\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}_{H_+}\oplus\left(-\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}_{H_+'}\right).
	\end{equation}
	Then $\Psi$ is an $\mathcal H$-valued distribution on $\overline{M}$, $K$ is a bounded self-adjoint involution on $\mathcal H$ with $\|K\|=1$, and the difference of $\omega_2$ and $\omega_2'$ is the sesquilinear kernel of $\Psi$ twisted by $K$:
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:difference as a K-kernel}
		w\equiv\omega_2-\omega_2'
		=\left(\Psi(\overline{\,\cdot\,}),K\Psi(\,\cdot\,)\right).
	\end{equation}
	Clearly $\Psi$ is dual-conormal, hence $w$ is as well. Similar to Corollary 3.11 in \cite{vasy_propagation_singularities_corners_2008}, where an empty Sobolev $b$-wave-front set means that the distribution is in $\mathsf{H}^1_\mathrm{loc}$, and thanks to \cref{lemma:ordinary and sobolev wave-front set}, it suffices to show that $\mathsf{WF}_b(w)$ is empty, for then $w$ is conormal to the full boundary of $\overline{M}\times\overline{M}$, and by dual-conormality it follows that $w$ is smooth on $\overline{M}\times \overline{M}$ (cf. Theorem 4.6.1 in \cite{melrose_differential_nodate} too). Indeed, if Vasy's $\mathsf{WF}_b^{m,\infty}(u)=\emptyset$ (with the obvious extended definition from the cases $m=\pm 1$) for all $m$, this means that the distributions $u$ is $H^m$-conormal to all boundary faces (i.e. in $\mathsf{H}^{m,\infty}_b$ for all $m$), for all $m$. This means in particular that $u$ is in $\mathscr{A}(\overline{M}\times\overline{M})$, so $\mathsf{WF}_b(u)=\emptyset$ in view of the relation between the Sobolev and ordinary $b$-wave-front set we established.
	
	For any $\chi\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$ we have $\|\widehat{\chi\Psi}\|^2= \|\widehat{\chi\Phi}\|^2+\|\widehat{\chi\Phi'}\|^2$, which implies that $\widehat{\chi\Psi}$ is rapidly decreasing in a cone precisely when both	summands are. In particular, thanks to \cref{lemma:properties of b-wave-front set} (e),
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:b-WF of doubled distribution}
		\mathsf{WF}_b(\Psi)=\mathsf{WF}_b(\Phi)\cup\mathsf{WF}_b(\Phi')\subset\widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}
	\end{equation}
	since both two-point functions are Dirichlet--Hadamard. Therefore, for any given covector $z,\zeta$, at most one of $(z,\zeta)$ and $(z,-\zeta)$ is in $\mathsf{WF}_b(\Psi)$.
	
	On the other hand, $w$ is symmetric. Indeed, since $\omega_2,\omega_2'$ are two-point functions on the same field algebra, we have by definition
	\begin{equation*}
		\omega_2(f,h)-\omega_2(h,f)=-\mathrm{i}\braket{f,G_Dh}=\omega_2'(f,h)-\omega_2'(h,f),
	\end{equation*}
	the middle term depending on the Dirichlet propagator alone and not on the
	choice of one-particle structure. Hence, denoting by $\widecheck{w}$ the flipped distribution $\widecheck{w}(f,h)=w(h,f)$, we obtain $w=\widecheck{w}$ after rearranging.
	
	Notice now that the proof of \cref{prop:properties of b-WF for HS-distributions} (d) works just as well to describe the $b$-wave-front set of $\Psi$. Indeed, the Cauchy--Schwarz upper bound for the kernel easily extends to cover the case at hand for a bounded operator $K$ (the only difference is that an extra $\|K\|$ appears in the estimate, and in our case we even have $\|K\|=1$). Thus, with a completely analogous argument we find, for any real-valued cutoffs $\chi_1,\chi_2\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})$ and any covectors $\zeta_1,\zeta_2$, an $L>0$ giving us the estimate
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:CS bound for w}
		\left|\widehat{(\chi_1\otimes \chi_2)w}(\xi_1+\mathrm{i} L,\eta_1,\xi_2+\mathrm{i} L,\eta_2)\right|
		\le\left\|\widehat{\chi_1\Psi}(-\xi_1+\mathrm{i} L,-\eta_1)\right\|\cdot
		\left\|\widehat{\chi_2\Psi}(\xi_2+\mathrm{i} L,\eta_2)\right\|.
	\end{equation}
	
	We now show that the $b$-wave-front set of $w$ is empty by employing the characterisation of \cref{prop:properties of b-WF for HS-distributions} (c). First, for any $z_0\in\overline{M}$ and any $\zeta_0=(\xi_0,\eta_0)\neq 0$ we find $L>0$ such that for $\lambda=\xi+\mathrm{i} L$ and all $(\xi,\eta)$ in a cone $\Gamma$ around $\zeta_0$ with
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:opposite pair bracket}
		\left\|\widehat{\chi\Psi}(\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\right\|\cdot
		\left\|\widehat{\chi\Psi}(-\xi+\mathrm{i} L,-\eta)\right\|\le C_N\braket{(\xi,\eta)}^{-N},
		\qquad\zeta\in\Gamma,\quad N\in\mathbb{N}.
	\end{equation}
	Indeed, we know that at least one of $(z_0,\zeta_0)$ or $(z_0,-\zeta_0)$ does not belong to $\mathsf{WF}_b(\Psi)$, so that at least one Mellin--Fourier transform is rapidly decaying while the other stays polynomially bounded.
	
	Consider now the case of different points $z_1,z_2\in\overline{M}$ and covectors $(\zeta_1,\zeta_2)$ with $(\zeta_1,\zeta_2)\neq(0,0)$. Since $\widecheck{w}=w$, \eqref{eq:CS bound for w} gives also the same estimate with exchanged $\chi_1$ and $\chi_2$ and arguments $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$. Thus, if both $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$ do not vanish, we find cutoffs $\chi_1$ and $\chi_2$, a complex line (using \cref{lemma:independence of the line}) $\Im\lambda_1=\Im\lambda_2=L$ and open cones $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ around $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$ such that, multiplying these two versions of \eqref{eq:CS bound for w} gives for $\zeta_1'\in\Gamma_1$, $\zeta_2'\in\Gamma_2$
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:product bound}
		\begin{aligned}
			&\left|\mathcal{M}\operatorname{\mathcal F}[(\chi_1\otimes \chi_2)w](\xi_1'+\mathrm{i} L,\eta_1',\xi_2'+\mathrm{i} L,\eta_2')\right|^2\\ &\le\left[\left\|\widehat{\chi_1\Psi}(\xi_1'+\mathrm{i} L,\eta_1')\right\|\left\|\widehat{\chi_1\Psi}(-\xi_1'+\mathrm{i} L,-\eta_1')\right\|\right]\cdot\left[\left\|\widehat{\chi_2\Psi}(\xi_2'+\mathrm{i} L,\eta_2')\right\|\left\|\widehat{\chi_2\Psi}(-\xi_2'+\mathrm{i} L,-\eta_2')\right\|\right]\\
			&\le C_N\braket{(\xi_1',\eta_1')}^{-2N}\braket{\xi_2',\eta_2'}^{-2N}.
		\end{aligned}
	\end{equation}
	Since $\braket{(\xi_1',\eta_1'),(\xi_2',\eta_2')} \le\braket{(\xi_1',\eta_1')}\braket{(\xi_2',\eta_2')}$ and $N$ is arbitrary, we find that $\mathcal{M}\operatorname{\mathcal F}[(\chi_1\otimes\chi_2)w]$ is rapidly decreasing in $\Gamma_1\times\Gamma_2$. The same estimate \eqref{eq:product bound} gives also the rapid decay if either covector vanishes, the other being necessarily nonzero. In fact, if for example $\zeta_1=0$ and $\zeta_2\neq 0$, then we find a line $\Im\lambda_1=L$ and an open cone $\Gamma_2$ around $\zeta_2$ on which either $\widehat{\chi_2\Psi}(\xi_2'+\mathrm{i} L,\eta_2')$ or $\widehat{\chi_2\Psi}(-\xi_2'+\mathrm{i} L,-\eta_2')$ (hence their product) is rapidly decreasing. We now choose a cutoff $\chi_1$ equal to one near $z_1$, the very same line $\Im \lambda_1=L$ and an open cone $\Gamma$ around $(0,\zeta_2)$, small enough so that $(\zeta_1',\zeta_2')\in\Gamma$ implies $\zeta_2'\in\Gamma_2$ and $|(\xi_2',\eta_2')|\ge c|(\xi_1',\eta_1',\xi_2',\eta_2')|$ for some positive constant $c$. Then the second bracket in \eqref{eq:product bound} is rapidly decreasing on $\Im\lambda_2=L$, with the first staying polynomially bounded there in view of \cref{prop:properties of b-WF for HS-distributions}. Thus, the Mellin--Fourier transform is rapidly decaying in $\Gamma$, and the case $\zeta_2=0$ is obtained by swapping the roles of $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$. It follows that $\mathsf{WF}_b(w)=\emptyset$, and the proof is complete.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- head-9: body_md -->
\label{sect:ultrastatic}

In this section we assume $\overline{M}=\mathbb{R}\times\overline{\Sigma}$ with the product metric $g=\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t^2-g_{\overline{\Sigma}}$, where $g_{\overline{\Sigma}}$ is a time-independent Riemannian metric on $\overline{\Sigma}$. We analyse the operator $P=\Box_g+m^2$ on $\overline{M}$, which splits then as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:wave op in ultrastatic}
	P=\partial^2_{tt}+\Delta_D+m^2,
\end{equation}
where $\Delta_D$ is the Dirichlet extension of the Laplace--Beltrami operator on $\overline{\Sigma}$, with domain $\mathcal D_2$. We fix the notation $A=\Delta_D+m^2$ and recall that, by Kato--Rellich, the powers $A^s$ in the range $s\in[0,1/2]$ are then defined on $\mathcal D_{2s}$.
<!-- end head-9 -->
<!-- prop-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:flat initial data}
	$E$ is dense in $\mathcal D_{1/2}\oplus\mathcal D_{-1/2}$.
<!-- end prop-4 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
The space $\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\Sigma)$ is dense in $\mathcal D_1$ since this is the domain of the Dirichlet extension. Since $\mathcal D_s$ is dense in $\mathcal D_r$ for $r<s$, we have that $\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\Sigma)$ is dense in $\mathcal D_{1/2}$ and $\mathcal D_{-1/2}$, too. On the other hand, $\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\Sigma)\oplus\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\Sigma)\subset E$, since a compactly supported function in the interior certainly satisfies the compatibility conditions \eqref{eq:compatibility conditions for homogeneous Dirichlet}. Since $E$ is a subspace of $\mathcal D_1\oplus L^2(\Sigma)$, we find the chain of inclusions
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:inclusions of spaces with compatibility conditions}
		\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\Sigma)\oplus\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\Sigma)\hookrightarrow E\hookrightarrow \mathcal D_{1/2}\oplus \mathcal D_{-1/2}.
	\end{equation}
	Since $\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\Sigma)$ is dense in $\mathcal D_{1/2}$ and in $\mathcal D_{-1/2}$, we conclude that the closure of $E$ is the whole space. This finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-19: body_md -->
\label{lemma:H^1/2-initial data gives H^1/2 solutions}
	Consider $(f,h)\in \mathcal D_{1/2}\oplus \mathcal D_{-1/2}$. There is a unique  $\mathbb{R}\ni t\mapsto u(t)\in \mathcal D_{1/2}$ solving $\partial^2_{t} u(t)=-Au(t)$ on $M$, $u(t)|_{\partial\Sigma}=0$ for all $t$, and $u(0)=f$, $\dot u(0)=h$. Moreover, $u\in\mathscr{N}(\mathbb{R}\times\overline{\Sigma})$.
<!-- end lemma-19 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
That we have a solution for initial data in $\mathcal D_{1}\oplus \mathcal D_0$ is classical, see \cite{evans_partial_2010}. By duality with respect to the symplectic form
	\begin{equation*}
		\omega_{\overline{\Sigma}}((f_1,h_1),(f_2,h_2))=\int_{\overline{\Sigma}}f_2h_1-f_1h_2 \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathrm{vol}_{g_{\overline{\Sigma}}},
	\end{equation*}
	we obtain that initial data in $\mathcal D_0\oplus\mathcal D_{-1}$ also give unique distributional solutions. By reflexivity, the complex interpolation method is compatible with duality (see \cite{bergh_interpolation_1976}) and hence the two endpoints interpolate to give unique solvability in $C(\mathbb{R};\mathcal D_s)$ for initial data in any $\mathcal D_s\oplus\mathcal D_{s-1}$, $s\in [0,1]$.

	Given the above solution, we clearly have $u\in L^1_\mathrm{loc}(\mathbb{R};\mathcal D_s)$ so that $u$ is an (extensible) distribution on $\mathbb{R}\times\Sigma$. By \cref{theo:smoothness and solvability in N'} we find $u\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M})$. The proof is complete.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
Let $\overline{M}$ be an ultrastatic globally hyperbolic spacetime with timelike boundary, let $H_+\cong\mathcal D_{1/2}$ be the one-particle Hilbert space as constructed in \cref{sect:qft}, and let $\Phi\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M};H_+)$ be the one-particle distribution. For any $v\in H_+$, $u_v\equiv(v,\Phi(\cdot))_{H_+}$ is a scalar, supported, normally regular distribution on $\overline{M}$ and is given by
	\begin{equation}
		u_v(\varphi)=\left(v,\Phi(\varphi)\right)_{H_+}=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt2}\int_\mathbb{R}\left(v,e^{\mathrm{i} t\sqrt A}\varphi(t,\cdot)\right)_{L^2(\overline{\Sigma})}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t ,\quad v\in H_+\cong\mathcal D_{1/2}\subset L^2(\overline{\Sigma}).
	\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:ultrastatic field is local}
	It is well known that $\mathsf{WF}(u_v)\subset V^+M$ in the interior. Moreover, the computation is always local. We will therefore prove that, after localisation at a generic point $q\in\partial M$, the past-directed directions in $\widetilde{V}_q\overline{M}$ cannot occur.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- lemma-20: body_md -->
\label{lemma:fourier transform in time}
	Let $\rho\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\mathbb{R})$ and consider its Fourier transform $\widehat{\rho}\in\mathcal S(\mathbb{R})$. Then, for every $w\in L^2(\overline{\Sigma})$ and every $\tau\in\mathbb{R}$, the $L^2(\overline{\Sigma})$-valued integral below converges absolutely and
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:time transform as functional calculus}
		(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_\mathbb{R} e^{-\mathrm{i} t\tau}\rho(t)\,e^{\mathrm{i} t\sqrt A}w\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t
		=\widehat{\rho}\left(\tau-\sqrt A\right)w ,
	\end{equation}
	the right-hand side being defined by the functional calculus of $\sqrt A$.
<!-- end lemma-20 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
The integrand is continuous in $t$ with values in $L^2(\overline{\Sigma})$ and is bounded in norm by $|\rho(t)|\,\|w\|_{L^2}$, so the integral converges absolutely as a Bochner integral. For $v\in L^2(\overline{\Sigma})$, functional calculus gives $\left(v,e^{\mathrm{i} t\sqrt A}w\right)=\int_{[0,\infty)}e^{\mathrm{i} t\omega}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{v,w}(\omega)$, and the complex measure $\mu_{v,w}$ has finite total variation, bounded by $\|v\|_{L^2}\|w\|_{L^2}$. Hence Fubini's theorem applies to
	\begin{equation*}
		(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_\mathbb{R} e^{-\mathrm{i} t\tau}\rho(t)\left(v,e^{\mathrm{i} t\sqrt A}w\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t
		=\int_{[0,\infty)}\left((2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_\mathbb{R} e^{-\mathrm{i} t(\tau-\omega)}\rho(t)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t\right)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mu_{v,w}(\omega).
	\end{equation*}
	The inner integral being $\widehat{\rho}(\tau-\omega)$, we see that the right-hand side is $\left(v,\widehat{\rho}(\tau-\sqrt A)w\right)$ by functional calculus. Since $v$ was arbitrary, the claim follows.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-21: body_md -->
\label{lemma:rapid decay of shifted cutoff}
	Let $\rho\in\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\mathbb{R})$ and $\widehat{\rho}=\operatorname{\mathcal F}\rho$.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item For all $\alpha,\omega\ge0$ and all integers $0\le\theta\le N$ we have $\braket{\alpha+\omega}^{-N}\le\braket{\alpha}^{-(N-\theta)}\braket{\omega}^{-\theta}$. Consequently there are constants $C_{N,\theta,\rho}>0$ with \begin{equation}\label{eq:bound for Fourier transform of time-cutoff}
			\left|\widehat{\rho}(\alpha+\omega)\right| \le C_{N,\theta,\rho}\braket{\alpha}^{-(N-\theta)}\braket{\omega}^{-\theta}, \qquad\alpha,\omega\ge0.
		\end{equation}
		\item Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space with
		$\operatorname{\mathrm{spec}} T\subset[0,\infty)$. Then for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$ there is a constant
		$C_{N,\rho}>0$, depending only on $N$ and $\rho$ and not on $T$, with
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:one-sided operator bound}
			\left\|\widehat{\rho}\left(\tau-T\right)\right\|\le C_{N,\rho}\braket{\tau}^{-N}
			\qquad\text{for every }\tau\le0 .
		\end{equation}
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-21 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
		\item Notice first that for positive $\alpha,\omega$ we have $\braket{\alpha+\omega}\geq \max\{\braket{\alpha},\braket{\omega}\}$. For every $N,\theta\in\mathbb{N}$ with $0\leq\theta\le N$ we then have, multiplying $N$ factors of $\braket{\alpha+\omega}^{-1}$ and using the above estimate, that
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:control on jap bracket of the sum}
			\braket{\alpha+\omega}^{-N}\le \braket{\alpha}^{-(N-\theta)}\braket{\omega}^{-\theta}.
		\end{equation}
		We have $\widehat{\rho}\in\mathscr{S}(\mathbb{R})$ as well, so for every $N$ we find a positive constant $B_{N,\rho}$ with $|\widehat{\rho}(s)|\le B_{N,\rho}\braket{s}^{-N}$. Together with the above estimate for $\braket{\alpha+\omega}$ this gives a constant $C_{N,\rho}>0$ with
		\begin{equation}
			|\widehat{\rho}(\alpha+\omega)|\le C_{N,\rho}\braket{\alpha}^{-(N-\theta)}\braket{\omega}^{-\theta}.
		\end{equation}
	
		\item Since $\widehat{\rho}$ is continuous and bounded, the spectral theorem gives $\left\|\widehat{\rho}(\tau-T)\right\|=\sup_{\omega\in\operatorname{\mathrm{spec}} T}\left|\widehat{\rho}(\tau-\omega)\right|$. If $\tau\le0$ and $\omega\ge0$ then $\tau-\omega=-(|\tau|+\omega)$, so \eqref{eq:bound for Fourier transform of time-cutoff} with $\theta=0$ and $\alpha=|\tau|$ bounds the supremum by $C_{N,\rho}\braket{\tau}^{-N}$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-22: body_md -->
\label{nc:lem:psi}
	Let $\lambda=\xi+\mathrm{i} L$ with $L>1/2$. Then $\psi_{\lambda,\eta}\in L^2(\Sigma)$	and $\|\psi_{\lambda,\eta}\|_{L^2}$ depends only on $L$ and $\chi$; in particular it is independent of $(\xi,\eta)$. In addition $\lambda\mapsto\psi_{\lambda,\eta}$ is a holomorphic $L^2(\Sigma)$-valued map on $\{\Im\lambda>1/2\}$.
<!-- end lemma-22 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
We have $|x^{-\mathrm{i}\lambda-1}|=x^{L-1}$ and $|e^{-\mathrm{i} y\eta}|=1$, so $\|\psi_{\lambda,\eta}\|^2_{L^2}=\int|\chi|^2x^{2L-2}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\mathrm{vol}_{g_{\overline{\Sigma}}}$,	which is finite for $L>1/2$ and manifestly independent of $\xi$ and $\eta$. The difference quotients in $\lambda$ converge pointwise to $-\mathrm{i}\psi_{\lambda,\eta}\log x$, which lies in $L^2(\Sigma)$ for $\Im\lambda>1/2$; dominated convergence upgrades this to convergence in $L^2(\Sigma)$, so $\lambda\mapsto\psi_{\lambda,\eta}$ is holomorphic there.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- lemma-23: body_md -->
\label{lemma:main estimate for WF_b}
	Fix $L>\max\{L_0,1/2\}$ with $L_0$ such that $\widehat{\rho\chi\Phi}$ is holomorphic for $\lambda>L_0$. Then for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$ there is a constant $C_N=C_N(N,\rho,\chi,L,m_0)$, independent of $\tau$, $\xi$ and $\eta$, such that
	\begin{equation}\label{nc:eq:main estimate}
		\left\|\widehat{\rho\chi\Phi}(\tau,\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\right\|_{H_+}\le C_N\braket{\tau}^{-N}\qquad\text{for all }\tau\le0,\ \xi\in\mathbb{R},\ \eta\in\mathbb{R}^{n-2}.
	\end{equation}
	Moreover $\lambda\mapsto\widehat{\rho\chi\Phi}(\tau,\lambda,\eta)$ is holomorphic in a neighbourhood of the line $\{\Im\lambda=L\}$.
<!-- end lemma-23 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
Let $\lambda=\xi+\mathrm{i} L$. The Mellin--Fourier transform of the compactly supported distribution $\rho\chi\Phi$ is, by definition,
	\begin{equation}
		\widehat{\rho\chi\Phi}(\tau,\lambda,\eta)
		=(2\pi)^{-n/2}\,\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt2}A^{-1/2}\int_\mathbb{R} e^{\mathrm{i} t\sqrt A}\rho(t)e^{-\mathrm{i} t\tau}\psi_{\lambda,\eta}\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t
	\end{equation}
	According to \cref{lemma:fourier transform in time}, this is the same as
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:MF transform in closed form}		
		\widehat{\rho\chi\Phi}=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt2}(2\pi)^{\frac{1-n}{2}}A^{-1/2}\widehat{\rho}\left(\tau-\sqrt A\right)\psi_{\lambda,\eta},
	\end{equation}
	all operators being bounded on $L^2(\Sigma)$ and $\psi_{\lambda,\eta}$ being square-integrable on $\overline{\Sigma}$ in view of \cref{nc:lem:psi}. Since $\|A^{-1/2}u\|_{H_+}=\|A^{-1/4}u\|_{L^2}$ we obtain a constant $C>0$ such that
	\begin{equation*}
		\left\|\widehat{\rho\chi\Phi}(\tau,\lambda,\eta)\right\|_{H_+} \le C \left\|\widehat{\rho}\left(\tau-\sqrt A\right)\right\|_{\mathcal BL^2}\left\|\psi_{\lambda,\eta}\right\|_{L^2}.
	\end{equation*}
	Taking into account \cref{lemma:rapid decay of shifted cutoff} (2), the operator norm of $\widehat{\rho}(\tau-\sqrt{A})$ can be estimated by $C_{N,\rho}\braket{\tau}^{-N}$ for $\tau\le0$. Since the norm of $\psi_{\lambda,\eta}$ depends only on $L$ and $\chi$ in view of \cref{nc:lem:psi}, we have shown the required estimate. The holomorphy of $\widehat{\rho\chi\Phi}$ is clear, since $\psi$ depends holomorphically on $\lambda$ and the operator applied to it is independent of the complex parameter.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
\label{rem:interior positive energy}
	At an interior point the same computation applies verbatim with $\psi_{\lambda,\eta}$ replaced by $\chi(z)e^{-\mathrm{i} z\zeta}$, whose $L^2$-norm is again independent of $\zeta$; \cref{lemma:main estimate for WF_b} then yields	rapid decay of $\widehat{\rho\chi\Phi}$ for $\tau\le0$, uniformly in $\zeta$, and therefore $\mathsf{WF}(\Phi|_M)\subset\{\tau>0\}$. Thus, up to knowing that the singularities of a solution lie in the characteristic set of Klein--Gordon operator (a standard fact in ordinary microlocal analysis), the proof of \cref{theo:Hadamard form of quantum field} below also covers the interior singularities.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{theo:Hadamard form of quantum field}
	Let $\overline{\Sigma}$ be a Riemannian manifold with boundary with metric $g_{\overline{\Sigma}}$, and let $\overline{M}=\mathbb{R}\times\overline{\Sigma}$ be the globally hyperbolic spacetime with timelike boundary with the ultrastatic metric $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t^2-g_{\overline{\Sigma}}$. Let $\Phi$ be the one-particle distribution constructed in \cref{sect:qft} for $P=\partial^2_{tt}+A$, where $A=\Delta_D+m^2$ for a positive constant $m$. Then $\mathsf{WF}_b(\Phi)\subset\widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$.
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
By \cref{theo:propagator is a solution} and \cref{cor:HS-valued N' is preserved}, $\Phi\in\mathscr{N}(\overline{M};H_+)$ solves $P\Phi=0$, $\gamma_0\Phi=0$, so \cref{theo:singularities of the BVP} gives
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:field is in the causal cone}
		\mathsf{WF}_b(\Phi)\subset\widetilde{V}\overline{M}.
	\end{equation}
	Since $\widetilde{V}\overline{M}$ is the disjoint union of $\widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$ and $\widetilde{V}^-\overline{M}$, it suffices to show that no past-directed compressed covector lies in $\mathsf{WF}_b(\Phi)$. The statement is local, so we fix a boundary point $(0,q)$, $q\in\partial\Sigma$, and coordinates $(x,y)$ on a precompact open neighbourhood $U$ of $q$ such that the causal cone is given by $\widetilde{V}U\simeq U\times \{(\tau,0,\eta)\colon \tau^2\ge |\eta|^2_g\}$. Choose then any open conic neighbourhood $U'\times\Gamma\subset {}^{\mathit b}T^{\ast}U$ of $q$ with $\Gamma\subset \{(\tau,\xi,\eta)\colon \tau<0\}$ and $\widetilde{V}^- U'\subset U'\times\Gamma$. This is achieved by simply enlarging the opening angle of $\widetilde{V}^-U$ by some positive $\epsilon$ in every fibre. Then we have $\braket{(\tau,\xi,\eta)}\lesssim \braket\tau$ in $\Gamma$.
	
	Choose $L>\max\{L_0,1/2\}$. By \cref{lemma:main estimate for WF_b}, the Mellin--Fourier transform $\lambda\mapsto\widehat{\rho\chi\Phi}(\tau,\lambda,\eta)$ is holomorphic near $\{\Im\lambda=L\}$ and satisfies
	\begin{equation*}
		\left\|\widehat{\rho\chi\Phi}(\tau,\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\right\|_{H_+}
		\le C_N\braket{\tau}^{-N}
	\end{equation*}
	for each $N$ with constants $C_N>0$. Since $\braket{(\tau,\xi,\eta)}\lesssim \braket{\tau}$, we deduce
	\begin{equation*}
		\left\|\widehat{\rho\chi\Phi}(\tau,\xi+\mathrm{i} L,\eta)\right\|_{H_+}
		\le C_N\braket{(\tau,\xi,\eta)}^{-N},
	\end{equation*}
	which proves the rapid decay along past-pointing directions. Since the only possibility is then $\mathsf{WF}_b(\Phi)\subset\widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}$, the proof is complete.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- theorem-19: body_md -->
\label{theo:existence of Hadamard states}
	Let $\overline{M}$ be a globally hyperbolic spacetime with timelike boundary, $P=\Box+V$ a scalar, formally self-adjoint, normally hyperbolic operator and $V$ a real smooth function. Let $\mathfrak{U}(\overline{M})$ be the field algebra of $P$ as defined in \cref{sect:qft}. Then, there exists a pure, quasi-free Dirichlet--Hadamard state on $\mathfrak{U}(\overline{M})$.
<!-- end theorem-19 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
We employ the deformation argument of \cite{fulling_singularity_1981}, see also \cite{drago_moller_2022} for a more modern presentation. That is, choose an isometric splitting $\overline{M}\cong\mathbb{R}_t\times\overline{\Sigma}$ with metric $g=\beta\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t^2-h_{t}$, $\beta>0$ smooth on $\overline{M}$. We will construct below two other globally hyperbolic spacetime with timelike boundary, the ultrastatic model $\overline{M}_{ult}$ and the interpolating spacetime $\overline{M}_{int}$. For the chosen time coordinate $t$, consider a past-cutoff $\rho\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}\times\overline{\Sigma};[0,1])$ with $\rho=0$ for $t\leq -1$ and $\rho=1$ for $t\ge 1$. For a fixed Riemannian metric $\widetilde{h}$ on $\overline{\Sigma}$, let $\beta'=\rho\beta+(1-\rho)$ and $h'_{t}=\rho \beta^{-1}h_{t}+(1-\rho)\widetilde{h}$ and define the new metric
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:interpolating metric}
		g'=\beta'(\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t^2-h'_{t}).
	\end{equation}
	For any choice of $\rho$ and $\widetilde{h}$, the metric $g'$ is Lorentzian, coincides with $g$ for $t\ge 1$, and is ultrastatic for $t\le -1$. Moreover, the covector field $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t$ is timelike and tangent to $\mathbb{R}\times\partial \Sigma$. We may choose $\widetilde{h}$ to satisfy in addition
	\begin{itemize}
		\item $\widetilde{h}\ge \frac{1}{\beta}h_{t}$ for all $t\in [-1,1]$, and
		\item the Riemannian metric induced by $\widetilde{h}$ on $\overline{\Sigma}$ is complete.
	\end{itemize}
	Indeed, if $\Theta(x)\equiv \max_{t\in[-1,1]}\sup_{v\in T_x\overline{\Sigma}\setminus \{0\}} \frac{h_t(v,v)}{\beta(t,x)h_{1}(v,v)}$, choose any smooth $\widetilde{\Theta}\in\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{\Sigma})$ with $\widetilde{\Theta}\ge \Theta$. Then we may construct $\widetilde{h}=\widetilde{\Theta}h_{1}+\alpha$ where $\alpha$ is any smooth Riemannian metric inducing a complete metric on $\overline{\Sigma}$. Clearly $\widetilde{h}\ge \frac{1}{\beta}h_t$ for $t\in [-1,1]$, and since $\widetilde{h}\ge \alpha$ with $\alpha$ metrically complete we see that $\widetilde{h}$ is also complete.

	We claim that the spacetime with timelike boundary $\mathbb{R}\times\overline{\Sigma}$ with metric $g'$ is globally hyperbolic, in that $\overline{\Sigma}_{-1}$ is a Cauchy surface. It is clearly everywhere spacelike, and we claim it is maximal. Indeed, let $c$ be an inextensible $H^1$-causal curve with respect to $g'$ and suppose, by contradiction, that $c$ does not intersect $\overline{\Sigma}_{-1}$. Since $t$ is a time function, we must have $c\subset t^{-1}(-1,\infty)$ or $c\subset t^{-1}(-\infty,-1)$. The first possibility cannot be, since $c$ is also causal with respect to $g$ and inextensible, and since $\Sigma_{-1}$ is Cauchy for $g$ it must intersect $c$. On the other hand, in $t^{-1}(-\infty,-1)$ $g'=\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t^2-\widetilde{h}$ so that the condition that $c$ is future-directed and causal is expressed, in the frame $(t\circ c,x=\pi_{\overline{\Sigma}}\circ c)$, as
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:future-directed causal curve}
		\widetilde{h}(\dot x(s),\dot x(s))\le |\dot t(s)|^2.
	\end{equation}
	Notice that the above inequality holds true only almost everywhere since $c$ is locally Lipschitz. If $c\colon [0,b)\to\overline{M}$ is future-directed causal, inextensible towards the future, and $c\subset t^{-1}(-\infty,-1]$, then we have $\dot t>0$ and for any $0\le s_1\le s_2<b$ we have
	\begin{equation}\label{eq:distance and time-separation}
		\operatorname{\mathrm{dist}}_{\widetilde{h}}(x(s_1),x(s_2))\le \int_{s_1}^{s_2}|\dot x(s)|\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} s\le\int_{s_1}^{s_2} \dot t(s)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} s=t(s_2)-t(s_1),
	\end{equation}
	that is, the Riemannian distance of $x(s_1)$ and $x(s_2)$ is controlled by their time-separation. Since $t$ is monotone increasing and $t\le -1$ in the considered region, we must have $t(s)\to t_\infty\le -1$, and \eqref{eq:distance and time-separation} implies that, for any $(s_j)\subset [0,b)$ with $s_j\to b$, $x(s_j)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $\overline{\Sigma}$. By the assumed metric completeness of $\widetilde{h}$, there is $x_\infty$ with $x(s_j)\to x_\infty$, so that $c(s_j)\to (t_\infty,x_\infty)\in\mathbb{R}\times\overline{\Sigma}$. That is, $c$ is not inextensible, a contradiction. It follows that $c$ must intersect $\overline{\Sigma}_{-1}$, that is, $\overline{\Sigma}_{-1}$ is a Cauchy surface for $g'$. By \cref{prop:properties of ghstb}, $\mathbb{R}\times\overline{\Sigma}$ is globally hyperbolic with $g'$.

	Let then $\overline{M}_{int}$ be the globally hyperbolic spacetime with timelike boundary $\mathbb{R}\times\overline{\Sigma}$ with metric $g'$ and let $\overline{M}_{ult}$ be the manifold $\mathbb{R}\times\overline{\Sigma}$ with the product metric $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t^2-\widetilde{h}$. That the latter is also a globally hyperbolic spacetime with timelike boundary follows since $\overline{\Sigma}$ is a Cauchy surface, by the same argument as for the region $t^{-1}(-\infty,-1]$ above. In the same interpolation region $[-1,1]$ we can also deform the potential by the convex combination $V'=\rho V+(1-\rho)m^2$. Therefore, on $\overline{M}_{int}$ we have the operator $P'=\Box_{g'}+V'$ which reduces to $\partial^2_{tt}+(\Delta+m^2)$ in $t^{-1}(-\infty,-1)$. On $\overline{M}_{ult}$, this form holds globally, so the analysis of \cref{sect:ultrastatic} applies. That is, the one-particle distribution $\Phi_{ult}$, satisfying $\mathsf{WF}_b(\Phi_{ult})\subset \widetilde{V}^+\overline{M}_{ult}$ in view of \cref{theo:Hadamard form of quantum field}, defines a pure, quasi-free Dirichlet--Hadamard state on $\overline{M}_{ult}$.

	The globally hyperbolic spacetime with timelike boundary $\overline{M}_{int}$ coincides with $\overline{M}_{ult}$ in a neighbourhood $U_1$ of a Cauchy surface sitting at a time $t=T<-1$ and not intersecting $\overline{\Sigma}_{-1}$. By the time-slice axiom, the one-particle distribution $\Phi_{int}$ constructed from $P'$ has there the same microlocal form as on $\overline{M}_{ult}$. That is, $\mathsf{WF}_b(\Phi_{int}|_{U_1})\subset\widetilde{V}^+U_1$. By \cref{theo:propagation of future singularities}, it satisfies
	\begin{equation}
		\mathsf{WF}_b(\Phi_{int})\subset \widetilde{V}^+{\overline{M}}_{int}.
	\end{equation}
	In particular, this is the case on a neighbourhood $U_2$ of a Cauchy surface sitting at time $t=T'>1$, not intersecting $\overline{\Sigma}_1$. Again by the time-slice axiom, the one-particle distribution $\Phi$ on $\overline{M}$ has, in $U_2$, the same microlocal form as $\Phi_{int}$. Another application of \cref{theo:propagation of future singularities} shows that $\mathsf{WF}_b(\Phi)$ only contains future-pointing covectors on the whole of $\overline{M}$. This proves that the pure, quasi-free state obtained from the one-particle construction on $\overline{M}$ satisfies the Dirichlet--Hadamard condition, and concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
If $\omega_2$ is the two-point function of the pure, quasi-free state constructed in \cref{theo:existence of Hadamard states} and $\omega_2'$ is the two-point function of any other quasi-free Dirichlet--Hadamard state on the Klein--Gordon algebra of $\overline{M}$, then $\omega_2-\omega_2'\in \mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M}\times\overline{M})$, with the difference solving the Dirichlet problem in both variables.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
\label{def:b-operators}
	For a manifold with boundary $\overline{M}$, the classical $b$-operators $\Psi^m_b(\overline{M})$ are the properly supported operators $A\colon\mathit C^{\infty}_c(\overline{M})\to\mathit C^{\infty}(\overline{M})$ such that, equivalently:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $A$ has a distributional kernel $k$ obtained as the push-forward to $\overline{M}^2$ of a distribution $K$ on $\overline{M}^2_b$, conormal to $\mathrm{diag}_b$ of order $m-n/4$, vanishing to infinite order at $\mathrm{lb}/\mathrm{rb}$, and one-step polyhomogeneous;
		\item $A$ is obtained as the quantisation $\operatorname{\mathrm{Op}}_{la}(a)$ of a one-step polyhomogeneous symbol $a\in \mathit{S}^{m}({}^{\mathit{b}}\!\mathit{T}^{\ast\!}\overline{M})$ satisfying the lacunary condition \eqref{eq:lacunary condition} in each boundary chart.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- lemma-24: body_md -->
\label{lemma:continuity of b-operators on distributions}
	Let $A\in \Psi^m_b(\overline{M})$. Then $A$ extends to a continuous operator on $\dot\mathscr{A}(\overline{M})$ and on $\mathscr{A}'(\overline{M})$. Furthermore, for each $k\in \mathbb{Z}$, $A$ extends to continuous operators from $\dot\mathsf{H}^k_{\mathrm{comp}}(\overline{M})\to\dot\mathsf{H}^{k-m}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\overline{M})$ and $\mathsf{H}_{\mathrm{comp}}^k(\overline{M})\to\mathsf{H}_{\mathrm{loc}}^{k-m}(\overline{M})$.
<!-- end lemma-24 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
\label{def:elliptic,characteristic,microsupport}
	Let $(q_0,p^0)\in{}^{\mathit b}T^{\ast}\overline{M}$ and $B\in\Psi_b(\overline{M})$ be an operator with principal symbol $b_0$ and full symbol $b$ (in some local coordinate system around $(q_0,p^0)$). We say
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $(q_0,p^0)$ is in the \textit{elliptic set} $\operatorname{\mathrm{Ell}}_b(B)$ of $B$ if $b_0(q_0,p^0)\neq 0$;
		\item $(q_0,p^0)$ is in the \textit{characteristic set} $\operatorname{\mathrm{Char}}_b(B)$ of $B$ if $b_0(q_0,p^0)= 0$;
		\item $(q_0,p^0)$ is \textit{not} in the \textit{microsupport} $\mu-\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}_b(B)$ of $B$ if $b\in S^{-\infty}(\Gamma)$ in some open conic neighbourhood $\Gamma$ of $(q_0,p^0)$.
	\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- lemma-25: body_md -->
For a finite open cover $U_1,\dots, U_k$ of ${}^{\mathit b}\mathbb{S}^{\ast}\overline{M}$ we can find $B_1,\dots, B_k\in\Psi_b(\overline{M})$ such that $\mu-\operatorname{\mathrm{supp}}(B_j)\subset U_j$ and $\operatorname{\mathrm{Id}}-\sum_{j=1}^k B_j\in\Psi^{-\infty}_b(\overline{M})$.
<!-- end lemma-25 -->
